Criminal Code
Several things have been admitted here today. One thing I should like to point out is that we in Canada have some of the finest legislation in the world for the protection of our consumers. We have our Food and Drugs Act, we have our marketing acts and we have our grading acts. All I should like to say is that any consumer who cannot read should get somebody to do it for him. I repeat that people are protected.
There is nothing new about trading stamps, premiums or about any of these things. They have all been in existence for centuries. However, it is left up to the individual whether or not he wants to accept them. When you buy porridge-and I will not mention the brand name-and they say they are going to put in a cup and saucer, what are you buying? Are you buying a cup and saucer or are you buying 16 ounces of porridge? That is your privilege.
I assume that the wife of the hon. member for Skeena has the same control over the purse strings that my wife has.

maintopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE OF PUBLIC OPINION GALLUP POLL OF CANADA
speechtext: Probably greater.

maintopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE OF PUBLIC OPINION GALLUP POLL OF CANADA
speechtext:
Like 90 per cent of the women of this country, my wife does the shopping for my family. The insinuation implied by the introduction of this private bill is that she has not enough ability to find her way down to the shopping centre. If we want to protect the consumer, we are going at it from the wrong angle. We should not tell the consumer, "You cannot go there". Nobody drags him in off the street. We have certain other angles from which we can attack. In its legislation the federal government today is protecting the consumers against adulteration. It is making sure that they are getting what they pay for.
We could approach the matter from another angle. What about all the zoning laws in the city of Ottawa? Some women have not the time in which to go all the way downtown. They are forced to shop in certain areas. I do not think we are going to gain anything by saying to the customer, "You cannot take trading stamps". You are not obliged to take them. You may leave them on the desk and forget about them.
As to trading stamps, they are not new. In 1952 the premium houses came out to Saskatchewan. They came to sell us an advertising deal. I am now speaking as a merchant. They said, "Here, we will set up a scheme for you. We will provide the stamps. Here are your premiums. It will cost you so much". As an individual businessman I had my choice. I really appreciate the criticism we are getting from that little

group over at the left. We have been told not only that many of us could not make a living but will never be able to make a living. In fact I appreciate their interest, but we are not the group that are asking for pensions. The basic thing is this. As an individual businessman I had the choice of accepting or rejecting that scheme. I made that choice and it was not based on nebulous reasons. I made it as a businessman. The question was whether it would pay me to spend that much money on advertising. It would not pay me, so I did not accept the scheme.
Now, I do not think that because I decide it will not pay me I should stop my neighbour from making his decision as to whether it pays him. If he loses his shirt that is his business; if he makes money, that also is his business. But I am so tired of being looked after by these connoisseurs, and I think a great many other people in Canada are getting tired of it too. We have just wasted a good deal of time, costing the Canadian taxpayer a good deal of money today, on an argument that the average taxpayer does not give a darn about.

maintopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE OF PUBLIC OPINION GALLUP POLL OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I imagine the hon. member for Skeena, (Mr. Howard) has had a great deal of edification today in the way his proposed bill has been debated. Before I give my views on this subject, I should just like to go back to a question he asked the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) with regard to whether that hon. member would be willing to have section 322 deleted, and some other sections too.
In order to set the stage, so to speak, for this, I would like to quote from the Canadian Grocer, the issue of November 21, 1959, which has to deal with an interview between the editor of that magazine and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton). It reads:
Mr. Fulton was interviewed by Canadian Grocer's Ottawa editor. His answers are clear enough in the story in this issue but they rate some emphasis because there is so much misunderstanding on the whole question-
The Criminal Code, including its provisions about trading stamps, is federal legislation. Its purpose is to protect against crime, which includes fraud and potentially fraudulent activities.
If trading stamps are inclined to produce fraud or fraudulent activities, then I suggest the Department of Justice will prosecute any company which is responsible for any such activity. But if trading stamps are simply another weapon in the free enterprise system in which one business competes with another business for customers, then

whether you agree with that type of advertising or not, it is still a very valid weapon to use.
The editorial goes on to make this point rather abundantly clear. It says:
Ottawa is concerned with the enforcement of the Criminal Code from the standpoint of preventing and punishing fraud. But it is inclined to stand clear of situations in which the code might be made the basis of actions in which the real purpose is not to eliminate fraud but to regulate business practice.
This is the intent of this bill. It is not to eliminate fraud. It has nothing to do with criminal activity. It is simply another way of regulating business practice. That is the fundamental weakness in the bill.
Much has been said about trading stamps. I know I am rather fond of certain types of dry cereals, but I am infuriated at the advertising on the box. You are always being asked to send five box tops and ten cents for a yo-yo, or some other toy. I would sooner have a reduction in price. But it is all right if that is the way they market them. As the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk) pointed out, some stores may increase their costs by putting in, for example, some parking space. Others employ boys to take the groceries to the car, and so on. They are all competing by giving service in different ways. They are all competing with their advertising budgets. One store may spend a very large proportion of its allowable expenses on advertising, and other stores may spend only half as much. Who is to say whether the store which spends only half as much is giving better value in the goods they sell as compared with the store with a very high advertising budget?
I think we all experience the situation where we go down town to a large department store to look around. I know when I go in that I purchase right away. My wife is a very careful shopper and she looks and checks all the prices. Time after time she will come back to small stores in our own neighbourhood and get just as good or better value than from the large departmental stores. It is just a question of how that particular businessman runs his business, whether his money is going into advertising in all its various forms and ramifications, or whether it is in the form of advertising by word of mouth, being passed on from customer to customer.
We live in an age when advertising is essential, when it is one of the foremost tools of business, and advertising is slanted to influence you to come in and buy. If I may come back to the Canadian Grocer, the Ottawa editor goes on to quote the Minister of Justice as saying:
Criminal Code
-the present government feeling is that the trading stamp provisions of the Criminal Code do serve their purpose effectively, although if it were later found that loopholes existed which might permit fraudulent practices, including abuse of currency regulations, then Ottawa would be ready to step in with necessary amendments.
This editor points out that this bill has no place at the present time in this house. This bill is properly a bill to be presented in the legislatures of the various provinces, as it has in Alberta. The other thing which the editorial makes a point of, and I think this is something to be considered is this:
This leaves the other provinces a choice of going along with the federal Department of Justice on its attitude toward trading stamps, or taking local action of their own.
Canadian Grocer holds no brief for trading stamps. As a business practice they are justifiable only to the extent that they may produce sufficient added business to cover their very considerable cost without price increases.
But if it is a choice between freedom to give (and collect) trading stamps, and legislation by lobby, we will take trading stamps any day.
That is the key to the whole editorial, that lobbies, whether on the part of supermarkets or on the part of other business organizations or what-not, require legislation, and this magazine, which is perhaps the spokesman for the grocery business in Canada, says they want no part of lobbies.
The editorial goes on:
Existing legislation, if properly enforced, provides very considerable safeguards.
Then it goes on to point out some of the other safeguards which we have. It says:
The Combines Investigation Act and associated clauses of the Criminal Code provides for suitable action to be taken where any practice tends toward monopoly, undue restriction of competition and freedom of enterprise.
That would appear to be a fairly effective weapon in the Criminal Code. The conclusion of the editorial is this:
There are no doubt occasions when business practices can lead to chaotic conditions and when some form of legislative form of control is required both in the interests of the public and the trade. But a state of mind which leans upon regulation to protect the protectable from the rigours of competition is not one that points the way to success in so-called free competitive economy.
The point which has been laboured by speaker after speaker is that this bill, and companion pieces having the same philosophy, is an attempt to legislate people into being good. They are attempts to mould us into the form of the particular group of which the hon. member himself is such a distinguished member. They want to make us all one. They do not want us to be allowed to make any mistakes. They want to regiment us, and they want to regiment business.
I am sure that all hon. members have received this booklet which sets out the case

Criminal Code
for discount stamps in Canada. It is a biased book, because it is issued by one of the trading stamp companies, but it does present arguments for both sides. It points out, as several hon. members have done in this debate, that the Criminal Code was amended in 1905, and it also refers to a publication which was issued by the board of trade in the United Kingdom-the report of a committee set up to examine this question of gift coupons and trading stamps. The United Kingdom report is in favour of trading stamps or, rather, the committee takes the position that a cure would be a greater evil than the one it would seek to prevent. Some pertinent points are made in that publication, and under the heading "Arguments Against Trading Stamps" the report says one of the objections raised is:
That the customer of a stamp-trading shop is misled by the inducements held out into believing that he is getting something for nothing, whereas in fact he may be paying very heavily for his purchase.
That objection has been mentioned today and hon. members have commented on the philosophy of "something for nothing". Well, people buy sweepstake tickets and go to bingo games. The lure of something for nothing is felt within the human race and no legislation can ever prevent people hoping for a lucky bet, or a piece of luck in a lottery or winning something from one of these companies. The report goes on to mention a further objection:
That many trading stamp companies offer poor value in the gifts which they themselves provide.
That argument appears to have been well refuted. The gifts are well known branded household names. The gifts are good, if you can get them. Again, the report mentions the objection:
That the retailer is frequently unable to escape from the trading stamp system even though he may wish to do so.
This, I think, is a valid argument because although we hear that an increased volume of sales will mean that trading stamps may be used at no cost to the merchant, if everybody uses trading stamps, where is the increased volume to come from? If a company uses trading stamps as a means of building up a business, will it not be forced to continue the practice in order to maintain that business? However, a company would in any case be obliged to continue other forms of advertising in order to maintain its position, or be forced to continue giving other forms of service if it wished to keep its business.
Another point which the committee brought up was:

That trading stamp companies are essentially parasitic, providing no useful service to the community in return for the profit which they make.
This implies that all who are, say, hucksters are parasitic; that all advertising agents and all those employed in advertising media contribute nothing. I would think that that is not a very valid contention, believing as I do that advertising has contributed to the development of a higher standard of living in Canada, United States and the rest of the western world. Finally, this objection is noted:
That the system oilers special temptations to fraud by ephemeral trading stamp companies.
If that is the case we have provisions in the Criminal Code which will take care of that situation.
The Economist, a well known British publication, summed up the case against trading stamps very well, in my opinion, in its issue of May 2, 1959. It had this to say:
The National Chamber of Trade's report strongly deplores stamp trading (and all other forms of cut-price trading), arguing that traders will lose money, that customers will pay more for their goods, and that only the promoters stand to gain. There is some truth in these statements, but probably not much. Traders will lose no more money through this form of price-cutting than another: the moment it becomes too expensive they will no doubt drop it, and return to conventional pricecutting, if not to uncompetitiveness. Should all retailers adopt stamp trading schemes, prices would probably rise slightly to cover their cost; but competition should keep this to a minimum, and most price cuts-in supermarkets, for example-are now paid for by quietly "loading" other prices. The stamp traders will profit from their activities, certainly; provided they give value for money, why not? The one thing which is most certainly true about stamp trading is that the actual savings to the consumer are not as great as they are made out to be: but this is true in many, if not most, aspects of retailing.
I think that last sentence puts it in a nutshell. These trading stamps are simply an ingenious scheme-a scheme which started some 70 years ago in the United States but which is relatively new here and in the United Kingdom.

subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1960-61

speechtext: A message from His Excellency the Governor General transmitting estimates for the financial year ending March 31, 1961, was presented by Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) and read by Mr. Deputy Speaker to the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MAIN ESTIMATES, 1960-61
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in tabling the main estimates for the fiscal year 1960-61 I should like to make a very brief statement to the house indicating to hon. members certain significant features.
I am pleased to report that compared with the estimates for 1959-60 tabled to date, a decrease of $164.9 million has been effected in the total of the non-statutory items for 196061 and that the over-all increase has been held to $58.2 million, an increase of approximately 1 per cent. This result continues the trend established last year in bringing about reductions in controllable expenditures. The very careful and detailed review of the estimates made by treasury board this year has permitted this reduction to be achieved without any decrease in essential public services.
These estimates provide for sustaining, and in some cases enlarging, the expenditures relating directly to national development such as atomic energy, exploration and scientific research, and transportation and communications. Other controllable costs have been sharply restrained.
I move, seconded by my colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill):
That the message of His Excellency, together with the estimates presented this day, be referred to the committee of supply.

On the other hand, on
the point of order which prompts me to rise at the moment, I believe the motion itself is not debatable.
I must point out to the house that last year the Minister of Finance greatly offended those in this party because he made a very lengthy statement at this stage in the proceedings, and the most offensive part of it was that he introduced the statement with the words that he was following the example of his predecessors in doing such and such.
Now, he did indicate that a statement such as he gave had not been given at least for some five years in the house. I want to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that on the previous occasions when a statement of this kind was made, it was given by one of his predecessors not with any attempt or design to have any political tub-thumping or self-praise, but on the contrary simply to point out to the house -I assume, having regard to the procedure, with the consent of the house-that the estimates as tabled did have some novel features in the style of the contents. The predecessor of the present Minister of Finance was quite terse in making any references to actual comparisons of expenditures, with those of previous years.
One has a great deal of hesitancy about speaking to the Minister of Finance in the light of what he had to say last week concerning the rights of opposition members to make remarks. One, of course, was reminded of that statement by one of the French kings, "L'etat, c'est moi".

speechtext: should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and I do so because of Canada's interest in world peace. speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CANADIAN STEPS TO MAINTAIN PEACE
speechtext:
There is, Mr. Speaker, on the northern border between Israel and Syria, a United Nations truce supervisory organization which has been active. They have requested each side to get out of the demilitarized zone. I understand the commander of that organization is now in the district checking to see whether or not this has actually been done. In the meantime both the United Arab Republic and Israel have filed a memorandum with the United Nations, but neither has asked for a meeting of the security council.
With regard to the Israeli-United Arab Republic border to the south, there have been no further developments. Apparently the rumour that a division of United Arab Republic troops had moved in near the border is not correct. We have received no reports of any serious developments on that southern border.

subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO CANADIAN STEPS TO MAINTAIN PEACE
speechtext: I have a supplementary question. In view of these developments, which I am certain are of concern to all of us and to all democratic countries, may I ask whether

any consideration is being given by the minister's department to the possibility or the necessity of recommending to the United Nations that the emergency force be extended beyond the Gaza strip and be a U.N. emergency force on all borders where there is trouble?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker; no decision of that kind has been taken. The United Nations emergency force was set up under the authority of all the member states in the United Nations, and it is fulfilling its function at the present time on the southern border. The truce supervisory organization is doing the same thing on the northern border. For the time being at least there is no need to take the further step suggested by the hon. member.

Perhaps I misunderstood the minister, and I should like to ask a supplementary question. In view of the fact that the United Nations emergency force has proved so successful on the Gaza strip, and in view of the fact that we are now probably facing a serious situation elsewhere, will consideration be given to the expansion of that principle and policy on other borders?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Of course, as the hon. member knows, Canada's policy has been to have one of the battalions of our regular army in Canada earmarked for service under the United Nations should the government decide that the need has arisen to take such action. That is the part Canada is playing in this regard at the present time.
One battalion?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: We think that is the practical course to follow, and the secretary general of the United Nations is of the same opinion.

I should like to direct a further question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, though it might perhaps be directed to the Minister of National Defence. The question is raised in view of the disturbances on the Israeli-Arab republic border. Are the Canadian members of the United Nations emergency force armed or unarmed?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING USE OF TRADING STAMPS
AMENDMENT RESPECTING USE OF TRADING STAMPS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-5, to amend the Criminal Code (trading stamps).
He said: Mr. Speaker, trading stamps have ofttimes been referred to as lotteries; and it was through the lottery system that luck arranged for this particular bill be drawn first out of the hat and thus provide an opportunity for a full day's debate on this particular subject matter. While I welcome my good fortune at having this bill being pulled first out of the hat in this type of lottery, nevertheless I disagree with the process used.
There is a wide ranging effect on the economy of the nation through the use of trading stamps and other similar promotional gimmicks, and I hope the debate which ensues today will be able to cover the pros and cons of the trading stamp question and other related types of promotional activities. I understand that in the gallery today are representatives of the Canadian Association of Consumers, who are most interested in this specific problem, and 1 hope the debate will also be of interest to them.
The design of the bill, without referring to its details, is that generally speaking it seeks

to amend section 322 of the Criminal Code which defines trading stamps and also provides certain loopholes through which trading stamps may be introduced and used in Canada. The purpose of the bill before the house at the moment is to plug those loopholes and make it illegal to use trading stamps anywhere in the nation.
This section, although not in its present form, was initially introduced in 1905. At that time the stamp promoters were attempting, through the use of trading stamps, to establish small scale monopolies in certain retail fields by confining the use of the stamps to particular stores. Also certain stamp companies in 1905 were nothing more than what we loosely refer to as fly by night outfits. That is to say, they would invade a certain area and embarked upon a sales campaign of stamps to individual stores; then they would fly the coop, as it were, so that when the consumer came to redeem his stamps there would be no merchandise for which to exchange them.
The history of the development of business enterprise and its activities over the years shows that there are certain trends which private enterprise takes. One of these trends is toward a monopoly or control of the markets for its particular product. Another is an ordinary trend toward bigness itself, whether it be in one field of production, such as aluminum, or whether it be in the many fields of production such as those covered by the Argus corporation. Then there are trends toward price fixing and restriction of production in order to maintain unnecessarily high prices. There are predatory price cutting practices designed to drive other competitors out of business, and there are deceitful and dishonest promotional and advertising schemes.
Trading stamps fall into this category, being a promotional gimmick. That is, in effect, part of a dishonest form of advertising. It also tends to assist in the movement toward a monopoly situation or oligopoly or control of the market within fewer and fewer hands. While the bill relates specifically to trading stamps and receipts which may be redeemed for particular merchandise, this is only a part of the over-all picture of what I consider to be dishonest forms or gimmicks in the advertising field.
Some argument is raised that the government or parliament has no right to interfere in, regulate, or control the operation of private enterprise; that is to say, private enterprise should have the opportunity, without interference or restriction, of doing whatever it pleases. But a review will show that every time parliament, upon the initiative of government through its prerogative in introducing

certain types of bills, has considered these interferences with or invasions of the activities of free enterprise, it has been prompted by governments which are partial to the free enterprise system itself; and the private enterprisers themselves have, by their activities, practically demanded governmental or parliamentary interference, regulation or control of some of those activities.
This interference with and regulation of certain activities of the private enterprise system over the years is necessary in order to protect the consumer against irresponsible or unethical business practices. We accept today as necessary parliamentary or government regulation against those practices in order to protect the consumer. The damaging effects that trading stamps can have upon our economy and the business world certainly call for such regulation.
The major damaging effect of trading stamps is that they accentuate this trend toward control of a market within fewer and fewer hands. The royal commission on price spreads recently gave us some indication how that trend has been developing in the grocery field. In fact, if I may, I should like to refer to one or two figures from the commission's report to show how this has been developing. For instance, in 1951 the percentage of the grocery trade which chain stores had was 37.2 per cent, and in 1958 it had practically doubled and was 64 per cent. This compares with the independent grocer whose percentage decreased from 62.8 per cent in 1951 to only 36 per cent in 1958, and should indicate the trend toward control over the market, in the grocery field especially, with it falling into fewer and fewer hands all the time while the activities of the independent grocer or businessman are declining. This trend will be helped, and is being helped at the moment, by the use of trading stamps. In this regard it represents not very much more than another nail in the coffin of the small business entrepreneur in this nation.
The argument is made that even though the small businessman may be prohibited from participating in trading stamp schemes himself, he can compete with these concerns which are using trading stamps in the matter of price; that if the small businessman wants to compete and does not want to or cannot use these stamps, then his answer is to compete in the field of price reduction in order to attract people to his particular store. This, of course, is rather an erroneous approach, because it relates to different systems or arrangements or concepts of what appeals to the consumer.
Criminal Code
Stamps in themselves have an appeal to the unknown-to me, at least-psychological desire on the part of the consumer to participate in saving things, or to play some sort of game and see how long it takes to fill up a book. It may be some desire to satisfy that inculcated attitude that we have of getting something for nothing by thinking that by saving stamps from a particular store you are able to get other merchandise, such as a floor polisher or something like that, free of charge. Price as a competitive factor cannot bear comparison or compete with the psychological appeal that trading stamps and other promotional gimmicks have. It is trying to relate two different concepts of what constitutes competition, and they do not fit together. In this field, the promise of something for nothing, even a brief look at the advertising material used to sell these stamp deals, the books issued by the stamp companies, shows an obsession with the idea that the consumer is getting something for nothing; that father is getting a free buggy, or that it is not costing anything to get a new bike, and so on.

speechtext:
If I may be permitted
to ask a question, would the hon. member state in the course of his speech whether in his opinion these trading stamps have the effect of increasing the price of food? If so, would he kindly indicate this?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING USE OF TRADING STAMPS
speechtext:
Yes. As far as I know there has been one survey conducted. That was made by the United States department of agriculture a few years ago, and covered the period from November, 1953 to March, 1957. This survey was conducted in 21 of the states of the United States, and it compared the price increases in stores using stamps with those in stores which did not use stamps. While I am not in possession of the complete report I have a newspaper reference to it which indicates that in those stores using stamps the price increase was .6 per cent greater on an average than in stores which did not use them. I have further reference to make to the question of the effect of trading stamps on prices, but perhaps the hon. member will permit me to follow the outline of my remarks first of all, and I will return to that question later.
There is no doubt, as I was saying, that we do not get anything free today. The consumer pays for the stamps or for the

Criminal Code
merchandise given in exchange for the stamps, in one way or another. Whether an increase takes place as a result of the use of stamps is difficult to determine. The United States department of agriculture survey to which I made reference a few moments ago indicates a figure arrived at on an average and in the face of general food price increases at a retail level. There is a thorough examination of this question in the report of the royal commission on price spreads, and it is almost impossible to determine what actual price increase is the direct result of using stamps.
One of the arguments used by those who have instituted stamp programs in their stores is that because they are an advertising and promotional gimmick, they immediately result in an increased volume of sales for the particular store using them, and that as a result of this increased volume of sales the store is able to absorb the cost of the stamp plan. This cost, I understand, runs in the neighbourhood of 2 per cent of the sales volume. If the volume of sales increases the cost of the stamp plan can be recovered.
But how is this increase to be procured? It can come only at the expense of the store's competitors. These competitors, then, in order to compete on the same psychological basis are themselves forced to introduce a stamp system. Thus, over a period of time the more extensively stamp plans are introduced the greater is the trend to revert to the volume of sales each store enjoyed before the introduction of stamp schemes. And once this condition is reached, if the volume of sales does decline, or if it remains, relative to other stores, what it was before, there is no other way possible than to arrange an increase in price to cover the cost of the stamp plan.
As to the stamp plans which have been introduced in the Ottawa valley, for example, all the companies which have introduced them invariably say they did so because they were forced to by a competitor, or because they were afraid that one of their competitors was about to introduce them first and they wanted to get the jump on him. I believe there is no doubt that even those major stores which are today using stamp plans would like to be free of this cancerous growth and merry-go-round. This is indicated by their own comments on this method of trading.
The royal commission on price spreads to which I made reference a while ago-I do not intend to read extracts from it because it is available to any hon. member who is interested-dealt thoroughly with the use of promotional gimmicks such as trading stamps,

and condemned them. It came conclusively to the opinion that this type of trading was detrimental to the consumer. There is no substitute for price reduction or price competition, no matter to what extent these promotional gimmicks are gilded; they are no substitute for lower prices to the consumer, which is the type of competition in which the consumer is interested.
There are certain forces in Canada at the moment which are engaged in promoting the use of trading stamps. These public relations activities are designed to show that stamps are good things and that we should use them, and that the federal government should not take any action to eliminate or condemn them. Sperry and Hutchinson which, I understand, is the largest stamp plan company in the United States, recently came to Canada and set up a public relations office in Toronto. I am sure all hon. members here have received material from Sperry and Hutchinson which answers a number of questions from Sperry and Hutchinson's point of view as to why stamps are a good thing and why they should be accepted by Canadians.
But the activities of this particular company and some of the people associated with it should make one wonder just what sort of public relations game they are engaged in. I would make reference here to Maclean's magazine of January 2, 1960, page 39. I hope this is a factual reference, because if it is not I am at fault in calling attention to it. I shall read the whole paragraph so it is in its proper context, even though some of it may not be really relevant to the point with which I am dealing. It says:
The CAC (Canadian Association of Consumers) is opposed, ironically, by Byrne Hope Sanders who once helped set up (for the wartime prices and trade board) a now-defunct network of women that was similar in purpose to the CAC. Now a Toronto research and marketing executive, she has launched a pro-stamp campaign on behalf of Sperry and Hutchinson, oldest (since 1896) and largest stamp company of them all-
And so on.
The reference I wish to make here is that Miss Sanders is engaged with Sperry and Hutchinson in a public relations job selling the stamp idea to Canadians. I understand that Miss Sanders is connected with another organization called the Canadian institute of public opinion, the Gallup poll of Canada. The Canadian institute of public opinion conducted a poll recently and in one of their releases dated Saturday, December 5, 1959 we find this with respect to stamps:
To find out the Impact of stamps in its varying degrees across the country-

They asked some questions. The Canadian institute of public opinion, I understand, normally desires to get unconditioned public opinion. It normally desires to phrase its questions so that they are not leading questions and are not designed to get a specific answer; but in its attempt to find out the impact of stamps in varying degrees they asked two very simple questions, which do not show the impact of stamps in any degree, never mind the varying degree. One question reads as follows:
Do you happen to know whether such stamps are given by any stores in this community?
I am sure this question does not elicit too much indication of the impact of stamps. The second question reads:
Is anyone in your family saving these stamps?
The answers are given; certain percentages are given, and I will not bother making reference to them. They relate to Quebec, Ontario and the west. The unfortunate thing, as I said, for the Gallup poll is that if this is being used to serve private ends, such as it might well be because of the connection of the same person with the Canadian institute of public opinion and with Sperry and Hutchinson, a public relations office, then the Gallup poll is going to fall into great disrepute in this country. We certainly hope that such questions as are mentioned in this Gallup poll are not going to be used later on and then have it said, we asked questions and public opinion favours trading stamps, or something of that nature. This is the type of conclusion one could easily come to because of the loaded questions that are in this release and because of the connection this one person has both with the so-called Gallup poll agency and the public relations concern of Sperry and Hutchinson.

speechtext:
At this stage perhaps I might make reference to the figures themselves so that hon. members can jot them down if they wish. In reply to the question:
Do you happen to know whether such stamps are given by any stores in this community?
The replies indicated that 65 per cent said yes; 25, no; and 10 per cent said they did not know. This applied to all Canada. In the maritimes, 30 per cent replied yes; 46 per cent replied no; and 24 per cent, don't know. In Quebec 94 per cent said yes; 2 per cent, no; and 4 per cent, don't know. In Ontario, 90 per cent said yes; 7 per cent, no; and 3 per cent, don't know. In the west- I assume that means everything from the Ontario-Manitoba border west; we always consider British Columbia to be the west- 14 per cent said yes; 65 per cent said no; and 21 per cent, don't know.
The answers to the question:
Is anyone in your family saving these stamps?
-indicate that in all of Canada 59 per cent said yes; 41 per cent, no. Those who said "don't know" were something less than one per cent. In Quebec, 80 per cent said yes; 19 per cent said no and 1 per cent, don't know. In Ontario, 50 per cent yes and 50 per cent said no. In the west, 19 per cent said yes and 81 per cent said no.
There was reference also to the fact that if parliament were to act as I am suggesting it should act on this bill it would represent an invasion of or a detraction from our freedom of choice. I suggest that when it comes to stamp plans there is relatively little choice. Many consumers are forced by circumstances as to where they live or how close they live to certain stores to deal with stores where stamps are available. Merely because they are available is another reason why choice is denied. I know it is said that this fits into the psychological pattern-I do not know what it is-to save things or to save stamps; that once a consumer embarks upon the saving of stamps his or her eye is then glued primarily to the catalogue and to primarily how long it will take him or her to accumulate enough stamps from a particular store- whether they be pink, blue, green or any other colour-to fill a book or 20 books that the customer needs to get a particular piece of merchandise. People will buy goods from particular stores because those stores have stamps of a particular colour and they need that particular stamp in order to get something they desire. Thus, freedom of choice,
[The Acting Speaker.]
of course, is watered down quite a bit when we take those facts into consideration.
I understand the attitude of the Minister of Justice is that this is a question that is within provincial jurisdiction and that the federal government should have nothing to do with it. It is unfortunate that the government is a bit lacking in courage if it adopts this attitude of passing the buck. If it is the government's attitude that this is a question that is primarily the responsibility of the provincial governments and that the provincial governments should take action such as Alberta has done to wipe out trading stamps completely, then the government should move to clear out this section from the Criminal Code. It should remove it completely from the statute books and make it entirely and purely a provincial matter. If the government did that we would know where we stood. If it is going to say it is a matter of provincial responsibility and yet retain on the statute books the present sections of the Criminal Code dealing with trading stamps then it is nothing more than buck passing and a lack of courage on the part of the government to face up to the facts.
I should like to wind up my remarks by saying that I look with anticipation upon what I hope will be a full ranging debate on this particular subject matter. I hope, sir, that you will be as lenient with other members who participate in the debate as you have been with me because I feel I have ranged a bit beyond the principle of the bill itself. I think you will appreciate, and I am sure hon. members will appreciate, that it may be necessary in this particular field to go beyond the actual principle of the bill and allow a fuller debate than would normally be the case at this particular stage of discussing a bill.
I wish to say that trading stamps and other similar promotion gimmicks, as I said earlier, are deceitful, dishonest and injurious to the consumer. They cannot be compared with price competition and price reduction because price reduction and price competition are the only types of competition that are beneficial to the consumers.
This is the most important issue that we have had occasion to concern ourselves with for some years. I say that not because I was fortunate enough to have the bill brought up at this stage so that it would be discussed but because I believe the principle behind the question itself is that important.
I have left much unsaid. It is not possible to make all the comments I should like to make because of the limited time at my disposal. I am sure also that other hon. members

will want to participate in the debate and will deal with additional aspects of this proposal. I have tried to confine my remarks to what I think are the basic principles involved in trading stamps and not to deal with what may be considered to be side issues. I think this bill is just as important as the one which the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) has on the order paper concerning capital punishment. I know that this bill is important in a different field and in a different way but I think it is important enough to warrant a vote by members of the house. I hope we will have a full and free debate and that the debate will end in time for us to have an opportunity to express by vote whether or not we are in favour of the bill. As I say, I think it is just as important in a different way as the proposal of the hon. member for York-Scarborough regarding capital punishment because trading stamps are a sort of economic punishment inflicted on defenceless consumers.

maintopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE OF PUBLIC OPINION GALLUP POLL OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the subject of trading stamps has engaged public attention I have been deluged, as I am sure every other member of the house has, with material, letters and advice, both for and against. A considerable amount of the material in favour of stamps has been furnished members by the Sperry and Hutchinson Corporation which I presume is a Canadian subsidiary of Sperry and Hutchinson Incorporated in the United States.
Nothing that I have read has shaken my conviction that trading stamps are another hand in the till of the retail merchant and another hand in the pockets of the consumers. Having said that as clearly and unequivocally as I can, the question remains, why should we try to prevent trading stamps if the public wants them? The answer to that is clear. Nobody wants to prevent the public getting what the public in fact wants provided, as far as our jurisdiction in this matter is concerned, that the criminal law is not contravened.
We are not called upon today to discuss the whole issue of trading stamps, whether they are good or bad or whether or not they are a help to the consumer and the retailer. What we are concerned with only is whether, using the bill before us as our terms of reference, all forms of discounts to consumers by means of what are commonly called trading stamps are of such a serious nature that they constitute a crime against the nation.
In this connection I should like to refer briefly by way of introduction to some of the material that has been submitted. I am well aware of the good work that has been done by the Canadian Association of Consumers in bringing to public attention the chief factors which are disturbing them in connection with trading stamps. The president of that association, Miss Isabel Atkinson, is well and favourably known in my own constituency. Another group which has been opposed to trading stamps is the retail merchants, both their national and provincial organizations.
I would say that the public has a right to be informed of the evils of trading stamps and of their uneconomic and costly use of time and money. They are uneconomic for the retailer because in addition to the staff of the store having to provide the service of

Criminal Code
displaying, storing and distributing the goods that the customer wants the staff also has to handle the trading stamps and this adds to the cost of doing business. It adds to the cost of the goods the consumer buys. I do not think it is possible to deny that.
I have heard the view expressed that the use of trading stamps reduces the cost of goods to the consumer because it increases the volume of goods handled by a particular store. I suppose it is possible for a cost accountant to -calculate whether or not trading stamps used by a particular store increase its volume to such an extent that its costs of operation go down and therefore it is in a position to reduce the cost -of its goods or to increase the benefits to its customers by way of trading stamps. However, the surveys I have seen, and which have been referred to by the hon. member which has just spoken, cannot in my opinion be held to demonstrate whether or not trading stamps on a national basis can be said to reduce costs to the consumer.
There are so many factors arising in each business which has been studied which contribute to the increase or decrease in costs, that I do not think it is possible on a nationwide scale to arrive at any conclusion from that method. We do know that if all stores used trading stamps the result would be an increase in cost to the consumer because this would inevitably increase the cost of doing business. The use of trading stamps, as I pointed out, involves the use of the retailer's time; it involves the use of a staff to carry out the distribution of these stamps; it involves printing extra material to be passed to the consumer, all of which has to be paid for by the consumer.
However, I believe we must direct our attention more closely to the bill that is before us. I want to do that, Mr. Speaker, and in that regard we have to consider what the field of jurisdiction of this government is. A press release issued by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) on November 3, 1959, contains this statement:
I do not for a moment minimize the objections that may be made to the economic effects of trading stamps. But in so far as their use relates only to the terms and conditions attached by a retailer to the sale of a particular article or articles of merchandise, there is nothing to bring such use within the criminal jurisdiction of the dominion parliament. From this point of view the only authorities who can control, regulate or abolish trading stamps as such are the provincial legislatures, acting under their exclusive jurisdiction over the laws relating to such matters as contract and the sale of goods.
The hon. member for Skeena said that this was merely passing the buck. He said that the government could clear up this

matter by removing the references to trading stamps from the Criminal Code and merely stating that this was a provincial matter. With the very greatest deference to the opinions of the hon. member for Skeena, I would say that our constitution cannot be disposed of in that way. It is not up to this government to say that this matter is no longer a matter of federal jurisdiction but is a matter of provincial jurisdiction or vice versa. Under our constitution, there are certain powers that are allocated to the federal government, and certain things to the provincial government; then again, certain matters are under the jurisdiction of both governments. The federal government is not empowered to pass this legislation and have that legislation enforced by the courts. We cannot simply do away with the constitution by saying this is not a matter for the federal government, or clear the field so that the provinces may work on it.
There is a federal responsibility in this field which has been recognized since the origin of trading stamp legislation in this country. That is legislation in the criminal field. In the earliest days, when this practice first became prevalent in this country, we find these words spoken by Mr. Kemp as reported in Hansard, 1905, volume V, column 9432. He attributed the necessity for passing this legislation to this -state of affairs:
Certainly some remedy should be applied to this abuse. These trading stamp companies, small and insignificant as they are, are permitted to do what no other kind of financial corporation can do. They are permitted to circulate money. This trading stamp resembles a postage stamp. They are sold at $5 for a hundred dollars face value. The merchant hands them out to his customer and they get into circulation that way.
Later on, he said:
The people who have been deceived into taking these stamps are generally poor people, and it takes them a long time to collect $100. Where the tremendous profit of the trading stamp companies comes in is due to the fact that the stamps are never redeemed. Then

when people present the stamps at the store, they will be told that the store is out of goods but some are expected in a few days, and in the end the trading stamp agents get away without paying anything.
This was a statement by one of the members at the time this legislation was originally enacted. It demonstrates the concern of the legislators at that time over the criminal activities of these trading stamp companies, and the fact that these activities should be removed. The legislation was, therefore, put on the statute books. Other matters were discussed at that time and most views, but not all, were in line with Mr. Kemp's views. Those discussions would indicate that it was

certainly the criminal activities with which the legislators were concerned. They were concerned with fraud and so on.
Mr. R. L. Borden, as he was before he was knighted had this to say, speaking to the legislators at that time:
Unless we are to proceed along a line of legislation that has not hitherto been proposed, it goes too far. But if we are to proceed along that line of legislation, it does not go far enough. To show that it does not go far enough, I have only to point out that under this law trading stamps may still be distributed and redeemed, if the person distributing is also the person who redeems, and if he redeems them at his own place of business. This still leaves untouched the element of lottery which was referred to in the argument of the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier)-and I am bound to say that that argument seemed to me to carry a good deal of weight.
It was, therefore, the opinion of both Mr. Borden and Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier that one of the main abuses about which they were talking was lotteries in the way they were carried out at that time. The trading stamp companies may have been conducting a lottery because the persons who procured these trading stamps would be left holding the bag by the premium companies. This is the situation to which the hon. member for Skeena referred and which led to the introduction of the section in the Criminal Code to curtail the distribution of trading stamps and that section is certainly one that commends itself to this house.
The bill in question here at the present time, however, in my view takes this matter right out of the criminal law and brings it squarely under the jurisdiction of the provinces because it relates to property and civil rights. In order to show that it does so, Mr. Speaker, I have merely to bring to your attention some of the defects or some of the arguments against trading stamps which show that undeniably this is a matter that is concerned with the regulation of trade.
This matter was investigated in England. The board of trade had a committee on gift coupons and trading stamps which reported in July, 1933. In the course of the report they summarized the arguments against trading stamps. If I may be permitted to do so, I should like to quote some of the arguments they summarized as follows:
That the customer of a stamp-trading shop is misled by the inducements held out into believing that he is getting something for nothing, whereas in fact he may be paying very heavily for his purchase-*
That many trading stamp companies offer poor value in the gifts which they themselves provide-
That the retailer is frequently unable to escape from the trading stamp system even though he may wish to do so-
That trading stamp companies are essentially parasitic, providing no useful service to the community in return for the profit which they make.
Criviinal Code
There is the further one which, of course, does come squarely under the federal legislation and which is covered by the present legislation. It is as follows:
That the system offers special temptations to fraud by ephemeral trading stamp companies.
Of course our legislation is specifically designed to get at people of this sort. The Indiana university school of business conducted a research into this matter and in their summary of conclusions, at page 118 of their report which was published in 1956, they outline some of the weaknesses of the trading stamp system which appear to be inherent and which I will set forth in order again to demonstrate that the weaknesses, apart from those that are already covered by the code, are matters of provincial jurisdiction. Here are the weaknesses as set forth in this report:
(1) the necessity of safeguarding stamps, (2) the reduction of market potential by premiums awarded to customers, (3) the inflexibility of a promotional program in which the cost varies directly with sales, and (4) the inability of operators to emphasize merchandise values, store services, and facilities.
The report goes on to state as follows:
In addition, other possible disadvantages of the trading stamp program for a specific retailer in the light of his store situation may include: (1) the prohibitive cost of stamps, (2) the necessity of increasing prices to offset cost, (3) the difficulty of discontinuing the stamps, (4) the possibility that benefits will be neutralized by a competitor's stamp plan-*
In other words, they all get them.
(5) the possibility that store operations may be hampered, and (6) the likelihood that advertising will have to be increased to promote the stamp, should strong stamp competition develop.
As I pointed out, Mr. Speaker, those are matters of regulation of trade, a subject which is not under the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. I should point out that the retail merchants are strongly opposed to trading stamps for three very good reasons. The first, of course, is that trading stamps which are defined by the code as stamps now are illegal and, second, that it adds to the cost of goods to the consumers or prevents reduction in prices which would otherwise occur. In the third place, trading stamp schemes are promoted by companies which are not in the business of providing goods for the retail market. It is therefore an encroachment on retail business by these companies that adds nothing to the service rendered or the quality of the goods supplied by retailers. I should point out, Mr. Speaker, that in recommendations of the British board of trade, they had this to say in their conclusions:
-it appears to us to be better for the retailers in any area to combine together to issue joint

Criminal Code
trading stamps, thus maintaining their independence, from outside competitive pressure, than to adhere to a scheme organized by a trading stamp company.
I do not really think that suits the Canadian situation at all. It is an observation made for action by a parliament which has complete control over all the affairs carried on in the British nation. We here are charged only with enacting legislation which is designed to come within the scope of our legislative competence at Ottawa.
May I for a moment now refer to what I consider to be one of the most serious aspects of these trading stamps as far as retailers are concerned, namely the fact that trading stamps represent an attempt by persons who have nothing to do with the retail trade to muscle in on the retailers' market. Those who issue trading stamps in contravention of the provisions of the Criminal Code, as I have said before, are engaged in crime. They demand a tribute from retailers and customers, promising in return to the retailer an illusory increase in sales and to his customer a premium which in value bears little relation to the toll exacted.
For reasons that I have mentioned in opposition to trading stamps in general I am glad that this bill has come before the house. It gives an opportunity for hon. members to express their views on the value or otherwise of trading stamps. But I think we must not be led into the position of passing legislation which would not be enforced by the courts because it is beyond our legislative jurisdiction. That is why I think it is necessary for us on this occasion to look more closely at the bill itself than has been done by the hon. member who introduced it. I have only these comments at this stage to make with regard to it.
The proposed amended definition restores the phrase "besides trading stamps commonly so-called", and it is not one to which I would take objection; but the deletion of the parts of the Criminal Code suggested in this bill would have two very serious effects, and they must be considered. In the first place, it would go beyond the legislative competence of this house; second, the bill the hon. member has introduced recites that "trading stamps includes... any form of cash receipt. .. given to the purchaser of goods by the vendor thereof... to represent a discount on the price". The amendment that the hon. member has proposed I think might well have the effect of preventing co-operatives from giving proper discounts to their own members, and that would have a most serious and disastrous effect upon the whole co-operative movement.
For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to have drawn to the attention of this house some of the disadvantages in the use of trading stamps, but I do urge hon. members to consider the points I have made with regard to the legislative power of this house to enact the bill which is before it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) made some very interesting remarks this afternoon when introducing this bill and, like other hon. members in this house, I very much appreciated his comments.
I also listened with much attention to the remarks of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Jones), who, if I understood him correctly, does not so much defend the trading stamps or the kind of promotion mentioned in the bill, as he disagrees with the hon. member for Skeena as to the means which might be applied in getting rid of this means of publicity.
Mr. Speaker, as far as I am personally concerned, I have always been opposed to that kind of publicity, to advertising involving the distribution of gifts in packages, or the distribution of trading stamps like those mentioned today. I have always been opposed to that type of publicity in all its forms. I refrained until today from public comments on this matter, or from dealing with it here in the house, because I wanted to study it thoroughly and satisfy myself that the position I would take in this house would be first and foremost to the advantage of the Canadian consumer, of the retail merchant and more particularly of the small retailer.
I wanted to satisfy myself, Mr. Speaker, that the benefits to the consumer from a legislation like the one introduced this afternoon would outweigh the disadvantage of a certain measure of government interference in private enterprise.
In the light of the present act, which was put into force in 1905 and amended when the Criminal Code was amended in 1953 and 1954, I studied the various briefs that were recently submitted by retail associations, by the Canadian consumers association, and also by the promoters of gift or trading stamps, as they are generally called. When I studied those records and those briefs, Mr. Speaker, I was astonished to find that the Retail Merchants Association as well as the various consumer associations of Canada were opposed to the distribution of trading stamps throughout Canada.

I was surprised, Mr. Speaker, to see that in our country only the promoters of trading stamp schemes favoured the system and this type of promotion.
And still, in the briefs submitted to us, I found that they had gone out of their way to try to convince us of the benefits resulting from the distribution of trading stamps. No more than the hon. member for Saskatoon was I convinced by the arguments presented in the brief submitted by the trading stamps information bureau, and published by the Sperry and Hutchinson Company of Canada Limited.
Mr. Speaker, what do the retail merchants, through the Retail Merchants Association, say in the brief presented by the association on January 7 to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker)? The Canadian Retail Merchants Association, under the signature of Miss Isabel Atkinson, stated in its preliminary remarks that, for some years, the Canadian consumers assocation had shown growing concern as a result of the increasing use made by retail merchants of promotional means which add nothing to the value of the merchandise put on sale, and which in no way help Canadian consumers to get better value for their money.
The brief went on to say that, at the annual meeting of that association the delegates representing consumers' associations from almost all provinces of Canada, since they represented sixteen regional associations, had expressed their strong opposition to the distribution of trading stamps across Canada.
And in the brief we find the reasons for which the association is opposed to a continuation of this particular type of sales promotion. Among the main reasons we find that some retailers object to this form of sale on the grounds that trading stamps increase distribution costs.
The second argument was that trading stamps have replaced low sale prices. The brief further says that they divert the consumers' attention from the value and the price of goods, that trading stamps are economic parasites and that their use tends to increase an already expensive publicity which misleads the consumer.
The brief adds that trading stamps deprive the consumer of the service offered by the retail merchant.
Here is what the Retail Merchants Association of Canada is asking, in the conclusion of its brief presented to the Prime Minister.
We ask that during the current parliamentary session, the existing legislation be reenforced so as to effectively prohibit all trading stamp systems in Canada, to rid our economy of this economic parasite.
Criminal Code
Now, what does the Canadian consumers association have to say? The chairman of the Canadian consumers association stated not so long ago, as quoted in Week-End, in January 1960, that "trading stamps are illegal, and that they add to the cost of products without benefiting the consumer."
A few months ago, I had the opportunity to receive from a fellow citizen in Montreal, who lives in the constituency of Dollard, a letter dated June 30, 1959. The letter was from Mr. Ivan Hamel who was drawing my attention to an item published in La Presse for June 23, 1959, under the heading "Readers Forum". The article signed by Paul Robi-taille, Q.C., dealt with the matter of trading stamps. He suggested an efficient way and a correct remedy.
The letter read:
On reading that part of section 322 of the Criminal Code, I am firmly convinced that the Canadian government had already legislated to prohibit and prevent that plague. However, some people resort to devious means of diverting people's mind from the existing legislation.
I believe, sir, that it is up to you to prepare and support all legislation which might bring about an adequate solution like the one suggested by Mr. Robitaille.
The letter referred to an article published by La Presse, under the signature of Mr. Robitaille, a lawyer, who wrote, on this same subject:
It is easily seen that merely by changing or striking out a few words the present practice of trading stamps would be made illegal.
Both the public and associations could therefore demand at once the necessary changes to rid us of those stamps which are unwanted by every body-including the merchants themselves-and which must surely contribute to inflation, because someone has to pay for those premiums: they are not free.
Mr. Speaker, on top of this evidence given by the Retail Merchants Association and by certain consumers, there is the evidence given by the Better Business Bureau which, as early as a few years ago, was asking the province of Alberta to adopt some legislation designed to abolish the use of trading stamps.
It would seem, therefore, Mr. Speaker, that promoters and distributors of trading stamps, in this country, are the only people who favour the system.
Some time ago, we received a document, referred to, a moment ago, by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Jones); it gives the reasons which seem to favour the maintenance of this system in Canada. That document does not seem to have convinced the hon. member for Saskatoon, nor has it convinced me of the desirability of continuing that practice.
Besides, I shall have the opportunity, later on in my remarks, to answer a few of the statements contained in that document.

Criminal Code
In order to introduce trading stamps in this country, their promoters had to by-pass the law and take advantage of certain loopholes in section 322 of the Criminal Code.
I should like to remind the house that, in May 1956, according to the same article I quoted a moment ago, from Weekend Magazine, an Ottawa businessman, Mr. Bertram Loeb, had a special study made of sections of the Criminal Code concerning the distribution of trading stamps, so as to make sure that he would not be brought into court if he had trading stamps printed and distributed in the stores under his control.
After a study made by Canadian lawyers, he managed to find a loophole which allowed him to go ahead with the distribution of trading stamps. He then formed a company, of which he became president, the Gold Bond Stamps Company of Ottawa. He has been conducting a thriving business ever since.
That is the result of that gap, of that loophole in our Criminal Code, and that is the situation which the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) would like to have corrected in introducing this bill.
If the bill were adopted in its present form, I believe the confusion which now exists, with regard to certain loopholes in the law, would be dispelled.
Some provinces have taken it upon themselves to legislate in this field. In 1937, the province of Alberta, for its part, amended the section concerning the trades and business act.
British Columbia, and more particularly certain municipalities of that province, that is, Vancouver, Victoria and others, objected to merchants using trading stamps, and the practice ceased at once.
In the maritimes, the practice is practically non-existent, but it does flourish in Quebec, Ontario and Newfoundland.
In Ontario, Mr. Speaker, just because of those loopholes in the legislation, the provincial government wants to make a test case with regard to the practice.
According to an item published in the Globe and Mail of January 28 last, the Ontario government is planning to make a test case on trading stamps circulating in this province. This is what the article says:
(Text):
The entire concept of trading stamps will be challenged in court for the first time in Canada in an action now being prepared on orders from attorney general Roberts.

(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, if this bill were passed, I think neither the provinces nor the municipalities would have to go to court to find out exactly where they stand in this field. The Canadian parliament has a perfect right to legislate on matters concerning Canada's Criminal Code.
If section 322 of the Criminal Code were amended so as to completely rule out the use of trading stamps in Canada, I think that would settle the matter and would eliminate the present confusion.
You may wonder what the consumer's reaction will be. I think the reaction of housewives, the main users of those stamps, would react in about the same way as this Toronto woman who, on hearing that the federal government was going to introduce a bill prohibiting the use of trading stamps, only replied: "I hope I can fill up my last stamp book before stamps are outlawed". In my view, that is the present position.
Retail merchants, just as the consumers, are very anxious to get rid of this bother, but as the practice is allowed in some provinces, businessmen have to compete, each in his own field, so, as an inducement to customers, they have to use that publicity gimmick. Then the consumer gets caught in a vicious circle, and seemingly prefers to buy from the dealer who gives trading stamps.
Mr. Speaker, my present position on this matter stems primarily from a desire to safeguard the interests of the Canadian consumer. In his remarks, the hon. member for Skeena showed us quite clearly, I think, that prices were slightly higher in stores using trading stamps. If we want the cost of living index in Canada to go down, I think one good way would be to eliminate trading stamps. It would greatly assist in lowering the cost of living in Canada.
While the primary objective is to protect the Canadian consumer, we must also protect the businessman, the small retailer who has to compete with stores that use trading stamps as a means of promotion. If the small retailer uses them, he has to pay for them, and the result may be that he will lose money, that his business will be less profitable, or that he will have to raise his prices. Again in this case, it is the consumer who foots the bill.
The reasons put forward by the promoters of such publicity methods, are, as I said, not sufficient to make us change our mind in the matter.

On page 6 of the brief which has been submitted by one of those promoters, whose name I mentioned a few moments ago, we are given a few reasons for which the distribution of trading stamps throughout the country should be favoured. The first reason advanced is that it is a painless way to save money for the consumer. The trading stamps are compared with deductions made from workers' cheques, to help them buy government bonds. Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any possible comparison between trading stamps and the amount our Canadian workers are made to save for the purchase of a victory bond. I also do not believe a Canadian taxpayer can be forced to economize if he does not want to; this is a personal matter and I think it would be antidemocratic to force a Canadian citizen to save if he does not wish to do so.
It has also been said that people who collect trading stamps are looked upon by their friends as good managers. Mr. Speaker, there is no need for me to tell you that this is a misleading statement. It does not hold water.
It has also been maintained that collecting trading stamps or gift certificates satisfies the instincts of people who like collecting stamps or antiques. There again, Mr. Speaker, I do not think this a sound reason. I am unable to imagine the satisfaction it can give to anybody to stick 100, 200 and even 300 stamps, all of the same size and all looking alike. To my mind, this satisfaction can scarcely be compared to that of a stamp collector who has come upon a rare stamp that was lacking in his collection. This stamp will be dear to the philatelist, whereas the trading stamps given out by the various dealers have no sentimental value, no feeling attached to them whatsoever.
Another reason given by the promoters, is that when they have filled their booklet, people feel deeply gratified when they go to the shop to sell it back. Well, Mr. Speaker, I wonder what sort of satisfaction anybody can feel who having collected enough trading stamps to be able to exchange them cannot even choose the kind of articles he wants, because the choice has to be made from a catalogue and he has to accept whatever he is given in exchange for the trading stamps he has in hand.
And other reasons are being given, emphasizing the pleasure, the thrill people feel, thanks to trading stamps, in getting something for nothing.
Well, Mr. Speaker, first of all, it is bad education for the Canadian people and,
Criminal Code
second, that argument is false, because the consumer who is in possession of trading stamps, has paid for them, since he gave money in advance to get them. In my opinion, it is easy to refute the arguments advanced by trading stamps promoters. But I will not elaborate on this point.
Mr. Speaker, housewives have told me they would rather pay lower prices than get trading stamps, since, with the money thus saved, they would buy what they want, where they want and when they want.
I do not think that it would be a breach of the Canadian constitution as mentioned a moment ago by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Jones), if that amendment to the Criminal Code were adopted. In fact, since retail merchants are now concerned with all the trouble constantly arising out of trading stamps promotion, due to the fact that promoters took advantage of a loophole in the legislation, it is therefore up to us and to the Canadian government to plug that loophole, and to adopt the bill which is now before us. The law will then be adhered to, and trading stamps will disappear, and nothing more will be heard about them.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that we shall hear other members express their opinion on the matter. I agree with the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) when he says he hopes there will be enough time left to allow members to express their opinion, tonight, through a vote, in order that this legislation may be adopted.

Mr. Speaker, I propose to say a few words in English because it seldom happens that I share the same opinion as my friends from the C.C.F. party and, more particularly, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard); but on this question I feel it is my duty to rise in my place and to acknowledge the perfect definition that appears in this new bill presented this afternoon by the hon. member for Skeena. However, when we read the explanatory note, we find that this bill has one purpose, namely to amend section 322 of the Criminal Code-and I quote:
The proposed amended definition restores the phrase "besides trading stamps commonly so-called", which was deleted in the 1953-54 revision of the code.
If we analyse this proposed change in the law, we find that it has now become necessary on account of the lack of interest, intuition and guidance of the former Liberal

Criminal Code
government which changed the law in 1953 and opened the door to this most disagreeable way of dealing with what are called trading stamps.
I do not want to condemn the members of the Liberal party who have spoken in favour of the abolition of trading stamps; however, I do condemn the former Liberal party, which was in power at that time, for not foreseeing the most amazing effect that this amendment of the law would have on the people of this country. Now that the harm has been done, we of the Conservative party are asked to vote in favour of a bill which I think deserves our most immediate attention and consideration. We are asked, as I said, to vote in favour of a bill which will correct this very deplorable situation.
Although I share the opinion of the hon. member for Skeena with regard to his main purpose of amending the law and having a ban put on trading stamps, I do not share some of his other opinions. For instance, he compared trading stamps to lotteries but I think they are quite different.
