I am sorry that I misunderstood the hon. member. On the other hand, I do share the opinion of the hon. member when he said that trading stamps tended to leave the control of business in fewer and fewer hands. I think that is exactly the purpose of trading stamps as they are used now. They are leading to a monopoly by a few. On this ground alone I think the government should pay attention to this question and the house should be asked to vote in favour of the motion.
However, I cannot agree with the member for Skeena when he said that the Minister of Justice lacked courage and was passing the buck in this matter. I think that the Minister of Justice has fully acknowledged his duty by interpreting the law as it stands, and I think that is also the way the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Jones) has interpreted the matter. We live in a free country, a democratic country and we are law-abiding people. We have full democracy and consequently the Minister of Justice in rendering his opinion on this matter has fully acknowledged the fact that we live in

a democracy and that no compulsory action can be taken. In view of the legal situation as it now stands, I think the Minister of Justice acted fully in accordance with the law of the country.
I will not give statistics with respect to this matter because I think the question of trading stamps does not need statistics. It needs good sense, and I believe that if we analyse public opinion generally as to this question we will see readily that the public generally want a ban imposed on trading stamps because they are becoming one of the main elements of our commerce and industry in this country.
(Translation):
My remarks will be brief, Mr. Speaker, on this matter of trading stamps. It is not my intention to waste the house's precious time in dealing with this matter, which I think requires most urgent legislative action. However, I realize that in expressing my views on this subject, I speak as a retail merchant myself, and also on behalf of thousands of small contractors or businessmen, in every field of trade, who are threatened with extinction by this system. I also speak on behalf of thousands of consumers who have become victims of this illegal trade practice.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I regard this situation as a threat to the very existence of small businesses across the country. I shall therefore show, for the consideration of parliament, first the way these trading stamps operate; then the producer's point of view; then the retailers' point of view, and finally, the consumer's point of view.
I shall try to set out very briefly the legal aspect of the question with regard to the federal and provincial governments.
Let us examine first how these trading stamps operate, right from the printing shop to the consumer. I think it should be stressed here that as a general rule, trading stamps are sold by promotion agencies to retailers. The retailers pay cash for the stamps and give them to the consumers, on an established percentage basis, in exchange for purchases. At the end of the line, the consumer who has collected a certain minimum number of stamps goes to the promotion agency and trades them for some merchandise.
As an illustration let us take the case of a Mrs. X who, having made a certain number of purchases, has managed to collect 1580 trading stamps. She goes to the promotion

agency and gets a piece of merchandise which retails for $15.80 at market prices. However, another person who has only 600 stamps is able to buy-I use the word "buy" intentionally, Mr. Speaker, to emphasize the monetary aspect of these stamps-merchandise worth $6.
Trading stamps, therefore, have a monetary aspect, which indicates that the use of trading stamps should be subject to the penalties provided in the criminal code against restrictive trade practices.
Moreover, if you look closely at the operation of these stamps, I sincerely believe they are a cause of inflation in Canada, and therefore should be abolished. Having paid for trading stamps the dealer distributes them to his many customers. Many of those customers must surely have lost or ignored those trading stamps. In short, the person mentioned a few moments ago, who obtained an article with a retail value of $15.80, is now the owner of an item for which the public relations firm does not collect $15.80, but $30.00, if not more.
Mr. Speaker, since nothing can be had for nothing; someone is bound to pay the difference between the actual value of the item and the price paid by the consumer. In fact, somebody does pay this premium. Since the producer or operator must necessarily make profits in his business, there is only one person who pays for those trading stamps, and it is the consumer.
The current uneasiness of retailers over the trading stamp system is even felt by the producer. I should like to quote an item appearing in The Rural Co-operator of October 27, 1959, under the heading Farm Business and entitled: "Who makes stamp money?"
(Text):
Trading stamps profit nobody but the companies that issue them and farmers should support demands to have them outlawed in Canada. We all like to think that we can get something for nothing but the trading stamps add to food store costs. When trading stamps add to food store costs they add to consumer food costs without any corresponding increase in returns to the farmer.
Food costs in Canada are not high in comparison to income. But consumers, led on by critics of agriculture, believe that food costs are high. This belief, supplemented by another unfounded belief that farmers are profiting enormously from today's food prices, makes it difficult for farmers to secure reasonable prices for their products.

The fact that an officer of a large supermarket chain last week called the premiums a consumer discount and stated that a 12 to 15 per cent increase in volume would cover the store's cost of providing premiums doesn't prove that consumers aren't paying for the premiums.

Mr. Speaker, this article gives a good idea of how producers feel about trading stamps.
As for the retailer, there can be no doubt about his desire to put an end to the practice.
Indeed, the retailers have become the very victims of that system of control by a handful of individuals. Then again, the practice places the small concern or the small retailer at a great disadvantage in relation to chain stores several of which control the printing, distribution and division of trading stamps for which they allow goods to people who have become their customers and find themselves under their definite control.
It is a form of economic coercion which places the small businessmen in the power of the big ones. Furthermore, I think that the practice is contrary to the public interest.
Even the consumer, Mr. Speaker, has become conscious of this undesirable position. I shall confine myself to one excerpt from the memorandum submitted to the Prime Minister, and published on January 7, 1960, in the magazine Canadian Association of Consumers. Page 2 of that report presents objections to that system and I should like, at this point, to read the more important excerpts:
(Text):
Trading Stamps Increase Distribution Costs
We object to these schemes because they increase distribution costs and thus increase the cost of living. They are a non-productive expense which widens the gap between the producer and consumer. Even if the claim were true that the increased cost due to stamps is offset by increased sales this could only be valid for a short period, and in particular instances. It cannot be true in the longer period when competing stores introduce these schemes. Food sales are closely related to population and growth, and no sales promotion schemes can make them rise suddenly in all stores in one shopping district.
In paragraph 2, we read:
Trading Stamp Schemes are Substitutes for Lower Prices
The royal commission on price spreads of food products drew attention to this point and stated in its report:	"In many instances promotional
expenditures are undertaken as an alternative to a reduction in price."
Criminal Code

(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, that opinion expressed by the consumers association fully explains the present situation and emphasizes the inconveniences of the trading stamps system.
The legal aspect of the matter, I shall let my friends, the lawyers go into. However, I should like simply to compare a statement made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) on November 3, 1959, with the legal opinion given by the Canadian consumers association, on page 1 of the brief submitted to the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker. And I quote that part of the answer given by the Minister of Justice:
(Text):
In the first place. If a trading stamp scheme in its nature or operation comes within any of the fields which are proper for inclusion in the criminal law, it would be the responsibility of the dominion parliament to enact any necessary legislation to deal with the situation.
(Translation):
I have therefore shown, Mr. Speaker, the economic drawbacks of this trade practice, and have also tried to show the house the various interest groups involved in this unfortunate situation of trading stamp distribution among the people.
Who, in fact, stands to gain from this system? No one, execept a small group of individuals who are striving to monopolize and control free enterprise and stifle healthy competition. Who, then, should step in? Should it be the federal government or the provincial governments? I am inclined to believe that under the circumstances, and in view of the monetary aspect of trading stamps, the responsibility for intervention rests on the federal government. However, it is for the house to decide on that point, but I think it is imperative that immediate and positive action be taken to put a stop to this practice which is deadly to normal business conditions.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I think trading stamps are a menace to the small retailer on the part of monopolizing supermarkets.
Second, the practice represents an illegal or illicit way of attracting customers to a specific store.
Third, the multiplicity of stamps cancels the desired effect while increasing the consumer price, whereas the alternative, i.e. unification, or rather the use of a single kind of stamp would constitute a monopoly.
I therefore ask this parliament immediately to take some positive and appropriate action to stop a practice, which I consider illegal.
[Mr. Valade.l
Before closing my remarks, may I be allowed, Mr. Speaker, to allude to the reports mentioned a few moments ago by the hon. member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau). On page 4 of the brief prepared by the Sperry and Hutchinson Company of Canada Limited we read the following:
(Text):
Q: If these discount stamps are legal, then who opposes them and why?
A: The principal opposition has come from merchants who do not wish to offer stamps and who are afraid of losing customers. In other words, the controversy over stamps has been largely a battle among merchants, some favouring free competition including the right to use stamps and others who wish to limit such competition.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, this is one of the most untrue statements I have ever read in any memorandum which is supposed to be sensible and which is supposed to come from business-minded people. I believe there are those who oppose stamps. I think the question in people's minds really is, are these stamps in the interests of this nation as a whole. Then, there are those who claim that trading stamps have left small businessmen near bankruptcy. It has been said that sometimes the ladies have been inclined to spend much more than they wanted to spend in these stores because of the advertisements for trading stamps. I think now is the time that this parliament should correct the wrong that was done in the last amendment to the law in 1953. This parliament should pronounce itself at this time by voting for the bill banning trading stamps from Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in this debate I should like to assure the house that I will, as usual, be very brief. It has been pointed out by several of the members who spoke previously in this debate that this whole idea of trading stamps is tied up in a very false scheme and that this scheme has been insidiously growing in this country through the idea of something for nothing.
It has been pointed out also by one of the previous speakers that there may be a little difficulty in classifying this practice of using trading stamps as being really criminal. I should like to point out that at least in one or two ways this is indeed a criminal practice. One of the things that this practice does, as has been pointed out by the speakers, is that it has built into our economic society a level of false cost. If we look across the world today and realize, as we must, the economic challenge that we are getting, and going to

be increasingly getting from the countries behind the iron curtain, I think all hon. members must agree that anything that builds a false cost into our economy is indeed very criminal.
There will be some question in people's minds as to whether or not the federal government should interfere with the freedom of choice of the individual. Some people feel the individual should be free to use his own judgment in this matter. I would agree with that if I thought for one moment that the individual was indeed free to use his judgment. But I do not believe that is the case. Unfortunately his judgment is likely to be based on the fact that he has seen only one side of the picture.
Modern advertising, both in this trading stamp field and in many others, has tended, I submit, to brainwash the citizens of this country from the time they are one year old. From the time they are old enough to watch television, to listen to the radio or to read a newspaper they are subjected day in and day out-in fact, almost every hour of the day-to advertising and promotion based on this false premise that you can get something for nothing. When do they ever see the other side of the picture and from whom do they get it? It is certainly not from our so-called free enterprise system because it is not profitable for anybody to do so. They certainly cannot get it from the newspapers, the radio stations or the television stations because unfortunately they have been dragged into the position in which they are dependent for their lifeblood upon this false advertising.
During a trip out west last fall I had occasion to obtain a copy of the Regina Leader-Post. I may say this was just about the time the report had come out from the commission that sat on the price spreads of food in the Canadian economy. An extremely interesting editorial or story-I believe it was an editorial-in the paper of that day stressed the part in this commission's report which said that the public themselves were to blame in that they tolerated this form of promotion which was increasing the cost of the products they bought. What I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, is that not only did this very newspaper as well as the other newspapers tolerate this system but they in fact promoted it. All you had to do was to turn the page and you would see on the next page a whole page full of advertisements which fell into the particular category which they were pointing out the public was at fault in tolerating. All newspapers and in fact all the mediums at our disposal in this country today to a great extent are obliged to depend upon this false advertising which is shown up so well in this trading stamp racket.
Criminal Code
If we cannot hope for any help in this matter from our newspapers and from our other mediums of supplying information to the public, then where can we hope to get some assistance? I submit that there is only one place from which the Canadian public can hope for any protection or for any assistance and that is from the legislators of this country, the people who make the laws. I would suggest that the best way in which to put a stop to this false premise of something for nothing is to make the practice illegal.
In the debate on the speech from the throne the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) pointed out the need for Canada to have a little bit more complete honesty with regard to world affairs. I would suggest that we carry this idea also into our own economic front at home. I do not think any hon. member will disagree with the statement that this whole trading stamp practice is-to put it kindly-dishonest. Since when, in this country of ours, is dishonesty not criminal?
I would suggest that the law already deals with the principle of trading stamps and that the situation today has come about because a loophole in the law was found. I submit that it is nothing more nor less than a deliberate attempt on the part of the promoters to circumvent the intention of that very law. I would suggest that the best way in which to deal with that situation is for this parliament, which makes the laws of this country, to proceed to plug those loopholes and to put a stop once and for all, if at all possible, to this deliberate evasion of the law.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one who has spent a considerable number of years in the selling field, both wholesale and retail, it is with great pleasure that I rise to speak on this bill.
I am also pleased to see the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) finally showing an interest in the competitive free enterprise system. His concern for the capitalist system, a system that has built up our industries in Canada until today we are the fifth largest trading nation in the world, and the interest he has shown in this system causes me to hope that there may yet to be a convert among the divided eight in the far corner of the chamber.
In the beginning, I wish to state most emphatically that I am against the use of trading stamps, and any other promotional device used by Canadian retailers which add nothing to the value of the goods offered for sale and which in no way help consumers when making purchases to get the best value for their money. Throughout the years all of

Criminal Code
us have seen these promotions in many forms, but their use is most widespread in retail food merchandising, with premiums inside packages, coupons to be redeemed on a specified product, and lately trading stamps calling for so-called free gifts. The increase in the use of this latter type of promotion has caused considerable controversy across Canada in recent months and I think it is fitting that this matter should be discussed in this chamber.
In my riding there are some chain store operators but there are also a large number of independent merchants who operate their own retail stores and are not affiliated with any chain. When discussing this matter with independent operators I found that their chief objection to trading stamps was the increased cost to their business, which must be added to the items sold, thus increasing their distribution costs and eventually the cost of living. Trading stamps serve as a non-productive expense which further widens the gap between the consumer and the producer. In reply to this argument some will claim that the increases in sales offset the cost of trading stamps; but if this claim were true, it would certainly be for only a short period.
After all, if any store in any village or town introduced a trading stamp program, and by so doing increased its sales, its competitors are not going to stand idly by for any length of time and see their business taken away by this type of program. It would not take them very long to institute a similar program, and therefore any advantage gained by one store having a stamp program of its own would soon be lost.
The original idea of forming food chain stores was to reduce the cost of retail food marketing. However, present trends would indicate a change from this policy of price competition to non-productive and costly sales promotions to attract customers. Another claim made is that trading stamps are free. This is, of course, deceptive and untrue, for the cost of buying trading stamps must be hidden in the price of the merchandise when it is sold.
In the beginning of my remarks I stated I was opposed to the use of trading stamps. However, I cannot vote to amend this act, for like so many bills which are introduced into this house by the C.C.F., I believe it to be a further infringement on our rights as private citizens and on the freedom of all Canadians. These socialists in the far corner have only one theme: There ought to be a law; there ought to be a law for this, there ought to be a law for that. They endeavour whenever possible to make changes in our

laws which would further increase bureaucratic controls and also cause further regimentation in Canada.
I do not believe that shoppers who like to buy stamps with food should be barred by law from doing so. The issuance of stamps by anyone is purely and simply a sales promotion. At the present time the shopper is free to purchase food from stores which give these stamps, or she can shun those stores like the plague. After all, sales promotions are not something new. For years soap companies have been giving coupons with their products; rolled oats have been packed with tumblerware, chinaware and silverware; and I well remember, when a salesman some years ago for one of Canada's large cereal companies, that the plain package was outsold by the premium pack by five to one. It was quite simple to see what the cost of the premium was by making a comparison between the retail price of the premium pack and the plain pack. Nevertheless, the premium package was the one that was selected by the majority of the shoppers. Even in popcorn little trinkets are packed, and I could mention many other promotions.
There are many who point out that the premiums secured with stamps are not free; the public is paying the bill. All of us know that you cannot get something for nothing, and while it is true that the public is paying for trading stamps, it is equally true that these stamps can be redeemed for a variety of valuable premiums. The promotion method may be deceptive, but it certainly cannot be called fraudulent.
There is an old saying that seems to be overlooked in the present controversy, and it is that the customer is always right. Today women do most of the retail buying in Canada, and usually they are careful spenders. Certainly this is the case in my household. Perhaps when shopping where stamps are issued they are paying more for the initial product. However, they are saving money, saving it in the form of coupons or stamps toward the attainment of some object they want, or believe they need. They of course are best able to judge whether there is a value in trading stamps, and I believe that if this parliament were to make laws to prohibit trading stamps it would be a restriction on advertising, a curb on competition, a limit to the benefits accruing from competitive free enterprise, and a further restriction on our individual liberties.
If this amendment were passed there would no doubt be short term rejoicing among independent merchants. But it is a reasonable fear that once the principle of limiting competition by prohibiting sales promotions was

established we could expect under this act or further supplementary legislation still further controls on competition. Certainly when reading the scope of this legislation as presently introduced there is every indication that there is little or no limit to the controls which can be applied. The amendment states, for example, that no trading stamps or any form of cash receipt, receipt, coupon, premium ticket or other device can be given to the purchaser which would represent a discount on the goods purchased.
I believe that implementation of this amendment could work to the detriment of independent merchants. These independents may not give away trading stamps, but in some cases they provide credit services, free delivery services, telephone charge accounts, entertainment in stores, free samples and free parking areas. All of these could be classed as a promotional sales device and give some idea of the regimentation of freedom incorporated in this C.C.F. amendment.
The government is being asked to be the official custodian of the shopper's purse, to direct the thinking of every Canadian, and eliminate the right of Canadians to decide for themselves the retail stores which give them the best value for their money. Like all other sales promotions, I believe that this fad will eventually run its course without the government restricting by legislation the rights of every Canadian of free choice in the market place.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to make my few remarks on this subject I realize full well, as do other hon. members of the house, that it is a very "hot topic" today. I might say I have considerable interest in it, being presently engaged in the general merchandising business, and also due to the fact that our firm once used these trading stamps. This is a question of very great importance, not only to those engaged in the mercantile business, or any business along that line, but also to the public across Canada.
Criminal Code
I may say that involved in this struggle which is going on today are not only the producers, the consumers and the men who service the goods in between, but also the trading stamp companies which have become a big factor in this warfare. The opposition to trading stamps seems to be stiffening all the time. Our own firm's position was that the stamps did not seem to accomplish anything. We were more or less driven into the field because our main competitor had taken up a trading stamp program, but after several months experience we both decided it was more or less a fraud at the expense of the public and we both got out of the program.
The background and history of trading stamps is as follows: they were started in the United States. I think Sperry and Hutchinson claim they first started them in Jackson, Michigan, in 1896, but there is evidence that they were also started in Milwaukee shortly before 1900. However, it is not the origin but the practice with which we are most concerned. The use of stamps spread rapidly at that time. It was a great fad, and all the confidence men who wanted to make a fast buck got into the act and a great deal of money was made in a short time by some unscrupulous people. The fad spread swiftly across the country around 1900 and things became so bad that in 1905 the parliament of Canada had to pass legislation banning the use of trading stamps. For a time this checked their use until about the year 1956 they began to show up again in Canada-they had come back some three years earlier in the United States. In the meantime, the people had forgotten in the course of a few generations the very unfortunate experience the mercantile trade of Canada had suffered during the first appearance of the stamps.
The present situation is that there is a determined effort being made by the trading stamp companies to flood the country again with their type of in-between merchandizing, and the Canadian consumer is caught at the present time in this more or less feverish competition of the chain stores, and the trading stamp companies are reaping the benefit of this competition.
Lined up against the present trend to trading stamps, are of course, a number of organizations including one of the most important, the Canadian Association of Consumers. This organization has, I think, about 26,000 members and there are another half million in 17 affiliated groups. I should like to read the names of these groups in order that hon. members may realize the type of organizations which are taking part in

Criminal Code
this fight against trading stamps. They are: Canadian dietetic association; Cercles de fermieres; Canadian federation of business and professional women's clubs; Canadian federation of university women; Canadian home economics association; Dominion council of the woman's association, United Church of Canada; Federation nationale St. Jean-Baptiste; Federated women's institutes of Canada; Hadassah organization of Canada; Imperial Order Daughters of the Empire; National council Canadian daughters' League; National council of Jewish women of Canada; The national council of women of Canada; Y.W.C.A. of Canada; the Salvation Army; Ukrainian women's association of Canada; and the Pioneer Women's Organization Inc.
I want to point out that this is a most influential group, very well organized and well informed on the problems of the Canadian consumer today. It is also one which is very interested in seeing that buying habits are protected. Their aim-and I quote-is: "to protect against promotional devices which add nothing to the value of the goods they sell and which in no way help consumers when making purchases to get best value for money."
Another organization which is also a large one and which is opposing this movement is the Retail Merchants Association which is made up of a very large number of independent merchants, from every province in Canada. This organization labels trading stamps "a parasitic innovation in the mercantile blood stream". Its very able president, Mr. David Gilbert of Winnipeg, explains that in endeavouring to get across this lure of something for nothing "they tell you the bargains available on stamps, not bargains available on food."
I might mention also that this stamp program has been opposed by the Canadian Congress of Labour which has through its chairman described the stamp program as "an attempt to levy tribute on the retail trade." I might mention also that two other organizations which have recently come out against trading stamps are numerous C.C.F. groups and the young Progressive Conservative association of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we rose at six o'clock I had been detailing groups of organizations that were at present 
taking strong objection to and fighting the trading stamp system. During the supper hour I happened to look up a couple of papers and I found several samples of the type of advertising one can expect under this and other similar programs. For example, I have one here with a number of pictures of dollars on it purporting to be coupons worth $5, $10, $25, and so on. Another paper I looked at had a full-page advertisement of one of the supermarket firms, and over one third of the page was taken up with the words, "Free 300 Stamps". It also has the picture of a smiling child alongside. These are just several examples of the kind of advertising that the public is subjected to under the trading stamp system.
Let me give a brief rundown of what the provinces are doing with regard to trading stamps. Last November the government of Alberta passed an order in council banning trading stamps in that province. In Manitoba the legality of trading stamps is before the court of appeal of that province at the present time. In Saskatchewan prosecutions have temporarily rid the province of trading stamps. Many cities are doing the same thing. Recently, the Vancouver city council adopted a policy of refusing business licences to those dealing in trading stamps. In the Gazette of February 1, 1960 there appeared an article headed:
Stamps mean higher costs, slow service.
The article reads:
The Quebec farmers association, in a statement issued Saturday, termed premium stamps "a malevolent form of promotion, harmful to both producers and consumers.
As a promotion gimmick, they serve only to draw customers away from one store to another. When all stores have stamps their net effect is higher cost, slower customer service and a larger part of price mark-up for stamp boosters", the statement added.
The inevitable effect of premium stamps, the association claims, is to increase costs.
"Stamps provide a form of competition between stores which is subtle and less likely to lead to real competition than price reductions."
Many other groups and societies have registered their strong objections to this reprehensible form of merchandizing. Mr. Speaker, the old saying is, "where there is smoke, there is fire". I submit that there is ample evidence that a large body of independently-minded citizens object strongly to this form of merchandising. The reasons have been partially covered by previous speakers, but I should like to go over a few of them.
Back of this whole movement is the pressure applied by the trading stamp companies themselves and, of course, this is backed by the motive of profit. A good proof of this is stated right in this publication called "The

Case for Discount Stamps in Canada" from "the information bureau on discount stamps" by the Sperry and Hutchinson Company of Canada Limited, 600 University Avenue, Toronto. It states on page 12:
Discount stamps are not a panacea for poor merchandising practices. But, documented case histories have shown that, everything else being equal, the retailer who operates a sound plan and promotes it properly is going to enjoy increased volume-and most important-increased profits.
This establishes very clearly that the main purpose of trading stamps is to increase profits. It is a very frank statement and, in order to attain those increased profits, some companies are ready to engage in all kinds of questionable tactics. This booklet also admits that trading stamps must increase sales by 12 per cent to cover costs. I quote from page 11, where the following question was asked:
How much must a retailer increase his volume for his overhead cost per dollar of sales to fall enough to offset the cost of stamps?
The answer reads:
Too many variables are involved to give a precise answer and it varies from business to business. But the average supermarket operator, for example, can cover this cost if he can increase his volume approximately 12 per cent.
In other words, once a chain of stores or a store enters into such a program they must increase their sales by at least 12 per cent to cover their costs.
Food chain stores themselves have disagreed on stamps. A number of them, with more courage and principle perhaps than others, have not been taken in by the trading stamps fad and they definitely remain aloof. Other chain store operators have admitted that they raise prices and others argue that they do not. One chain store executive said: "These gimmicks are nothing but parasites preying on the public gullibility". Another commented: "It is like a disease, a cancer that just keeps growing".
It is generally agreed that the customers themselves will pay 2 per cent additional costs where such plans are in operation. Sometimes the prices may be lowered temporarily in certain areas, but when everybody gets into the trading stamp plan, which so often happens as a result of the merry-go-round, the customer does pay that extra 2 per cent, and the only one who really profits is probably the trading stamp company at the back of it.
The royal commission on price spreads had a great deal to say about the fact that the public is paying extra for continually increasing packaging and processing charges before the sales are made. There has been no increase to farmers and fishermen, the primary producers who initiate the products in 79951-0-471
Criminal Code
the first place, whom many of us represent and wish to assist and who deserve every assistance possible. Trading stamps are added, often unnecessarily, like fancy and eye-catching packaging, to the cost of the product and the ultimate increased cost to the consumer. It is no wonder under these circumstances that the Canadian Association of Consumers and other organizations are waging an all-out battle against the false representation of trading stamp programs. It is true that these campaigns are luring a great number of adherents but that, of course, does not by any means mean that they are right.
I hope that the compaign being waged by the Canadian Association of Consumers will be eminently successful in combating this menace. The whole merchandising and retailing field would be better off if it could be rid of this nefarious practice. It has been amply shown that trading stamp programs are based essentially on misrepresentation. They hold down the price to the producer by gobbling up the additional price spread when prices go up. They add to the servicing cost and often are a substitute for lower prices. They tend to confuse the buying public on proper values and often deprive consumers of necessary services when the costs of trading stamp plans are added to the product.
All in all, the buying public would be far better off in the long run, even if they do not realize it at the present time, although I think they will catch on before too long, if all trading stamp and similar programs were eliminated. And if the retailer and consumer were to combine so as to realize the ultimate satisfactory condition in that field where the merchant gives-and the customer receives the maximum of quality and service for his or her dollar when this great mirage of trading stamp programs is removed completely from the scene.
Mr. J. P. Deschatelets (Maisonneuve-
Rosemoni): Mr. Speaker, for a few minutes I should like to consider certain aspects of Bill No. C-5 in connection with the amendment of section 322 of the Criminal Code respecting trading stamps. The question of trading stamps has aroused a great interest among the public and at this point I might underline immediately the strong attitude taken by the Canadian Association of Consumers, as reported by the Toronto Star in their issue of January 12 where they say:
We object to these schemes because they increase distribution costs and thus increase the cost of living.
This brings up a very important question. Do trading stamps in fact have the result of increasing the price to the consumer? At this time of unemployment and tight money,

Criminal Code
when more than half a million Canadians are living on unemployment insurance benefits, this is really a matter of great importance. If it is so, I do not think we should tolerate a system which has the result of increasing the cost of living.
I would have hoped that the government would have already investigated and brought this fact to light through a special committee which could also have examined the practice of giving away gifts and toys with the purchase of certain goods as is done today nearly everywhere in Canada. I suspect personally that such gifts and premiums are in the end paid for by the consumers. These are practices which it would be worth while to investigate in the interests of Canadian consumers.
But Bill No. C-5 is in fact a minor amendment to the provisions of section 322 of the Criminal Code. I have the impression that most Canadians have thought that since 1905 trading stamps were prohibited under the provisions of section 322 of the Criminal Code. It might be that at the time of the revision of the Criminal Code in 1953 a gate was opened to trading stamps. This is left to be proved.
But there is no doubt that an important controversy has developed between the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) and the majority of the attorneys general of the provinces as to their mutual responsibility with respect to trading stamps. It seems that the position taken by the Minister of Justice is that the regulation of the contractual aspect of trading stamps between merchants and consumers is strictly a provincial responsibility. On the other hand, the attorney general of Ontario, Mr. Kelso Roberts, in the Ottawa Citizen of November 30, 1959 is reported to have said "that there is no particular piece of legislation in Ontario concerning trading stamps and that the responsibility remains with the federal government."
The attorney general of the province of Quebec has also expressed the same views in a recent interview on television. In the meantime, a certain portion of public opinion firmly believes that there is a blanket prohibition in the Criminal Code concerning trading stamps. Unless something is done immediately to clarify this situation, we are going nowhere but into a state of complete confusion.
In view of the fact that we are dealing here with a very important matter, a matter which affects most Canadians because it concerns the cost of living and the price of food, and because also of the opposing views expressed by the Minister of Justice and the attorneys general of most provinces, I think

the government of Canada should take the lead in helping to clarify the confused situation. This is of course a personal opinion but I think that the smoothest and quickest way of doing so is by way of a reference to the Supreme Court of Canada. The government of Canada and the attorneys general of each of the provinces would have an opportunity, through their local agent, to go before the supreme court to discuss two or three questions that might be prepared by the able officers of the Minister of Justice. Ultimately, we would be in a position to obtain the opinion of the highest court on the following questions: I do not pretend, of course, that I have here covered in two questions the main points to be clarified. I do believe the questions prepared by the minister's officers could be along these lines:
First, are the contractual aspects of trading stamps, in so far as merchants and customers are concerned, strictly a provincial responsibility?
Second, does the enactment of legislation prohibiting trading stamps fall within the jurisdiction of the federal or provincial government? The results of a reference of that kind to the Supreme Court of Canada would be the first step in clarifying the responsibilities of the federal and provincial governments in this matter of trading stamps. The governments concerned would, therefore, be able to ascertain, quickly and without any discussion, their respective jurisdictions in that field, and thereafter it should be easy to tackle this problem of trading stamps.
However, if the Minister of Justice or one of his colleagues refuses to take advantage of the opportunity provided by this bill to give such a lead, to give a clear indication of the intentions of the government toward this important problem, then, Mr. Speaker, this government can be assured that hundreds of thousands of Canadians will resent this lack of leadership.

speechtext:
In the course of this debate, Mr. Speaker, the preponderance of opinion appears to be against the use of trading stamps. Some members have indicated that although for various reasons they do not favour the bill as an effective deterrent to the use of these stamps, others accept the bill as it is presented to us as a means of eliminating trading stamps from use in current mercantile practice in the promotion and merchandising of goods. I think, for my own part, that my opinion runs almost parallel with that of the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Crouse), who indicated his personal dislike of trading stamps but also expressed some doubt

as to the advisability and wisdom of endeavouring to pass legislation against one single aspect, one single manifestation of the promotional techniques of modern merchandising.
I believe there is another point that we should take into account, something which I do not believe has been taken sufficiently into account by associations of merchants in the country, by consumer organizations and others, and that is this increasing desire to go to the government to regulate and restrain business practices. I find, for my own part, that I am increasingly concerned at the possibility that, if all levels of business are going to continue to go to governments and say, you must protect us against ourselves, we will succeed finally in strangling entirely what we choose to call free enterprise, if we have it now. There must be some regard for the possibility that business itself and those who are opposed to this type of promotional practice have a responsibility to get across to the public, by every means at their disposal, by all forms of public education, the undesirable features of trading stamps practice.
I am not sure in my own mind that the government can continue to pass enforceable laws on every possible occasion that some particular division of business or industry feels its interests are being damaged. There is a great mass of laws on the statute books now which have fallen into complete disrepute in the minds of the public because the public does not believe they are desirable and people have no desire to obey them. I can think of one law which we have now that is flouted quite widely throughout the country because the public does not believe in it. I refer to our law regarding lotteries, sweepstakes and gambling of that sort. If we were to check up on the practices rather than pay attention to the protestations on the matter, we would find the law is being completely disregarded by a very large number of Canadians.
I should like to refer to the list of names of organizations read by the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Macdonald) which have indicated their opposition to trading stamps. I have no doubt in my own mind that if I were to go downtown in Ottawa on Saturday morning to one of the large supermarkets I could find members of every one of those organizations purchasing their week-end provisions in a store that gives trading stamps. These are matters which must be considered when we are discussing a bill of this kind and when we are asked to consider whether or not it will do an effective job of protecting the public.
My own belief is that the public must surely by now know that if they patronize a
Criminal Code
store offering trading stamps the cost of those trading stamps and premiums is contained in the mark-up on the merchandise which they purchase. There is nowhere else from which that cost can come. It must be there. If the public is prepared to pay that mark-up in the cost of the article they buy in the store, accepting as part of the price the premium stamps or premiums of some kind or another, I feel it is the right of the public to make that decision for themselves. It may be more desirable for the store offering stamps to say in its advertising, if you do not want to take the stamps you can have the equivalent in a cash discount. I understand that is not done, but that is not to say, of course, that it might not be done. This is a possibility that might develop. But it is true also that the majority of the public who now buy in stores offering trading stamps have the opportunity of buying in stores that do not offer them. As long as this opportunity exists, it cannot be fairly said that anybody is being forced into dealing with merchants who offer trading stamps. There is not, therefore, any undesirable influence being exerted on the buying public.
However, on the other side of the picture, Mr. Speaker, I think we must emphasize that there are dangers in the trading stamp philosophy of merchandising, in this promotional type of advertising, these massive promotions which the general public now accepts and which, if they were to stop to consider, they should avoid on every occasion.
I think of instances of which I have been told where producers have been brought under influence to sell products-farm products in particular-to large chain operations at reduced prices in order to provide the chain organizations with the opportunity of offering specials. The chain store or the large supermarket concerned very often says that it is giving to the public a special at a very greatly reduced price. But you often find it is not the store that is giving the special at all; it is the man who supplied the store with the produce in the first place.
This situation works a hardship on certain branches of our manufacturing industries, processing industries and farm producers. But I think these things can be corrected only by an understanding on the part of the public of all the factors involved in the use of trading stamps, by an understanding on the part of the suppliers to the large organizations that it is perhaps not in their own best interests to become involved in contractual agreements whereby they must provide produce at prices which make possible the use of the trading stamp as a mass promotional device.

Criminal Code
I think that somehow or other educational programs must be undertaken by consumer organizations, the retail merchants of Canada, better business bureaux and others, in order to give the public some idea of how they may estimate for themselves whether they are securing good value for the money they spend. Very often it is now extremely difficult to determine. At the same time I think that we here in this House of Commons must be very careful about how we try to wrap the public up in cotton wool perhaps against the public's own desires and to protect it from itself.
This is the very same public to which, every four or five years, we come back and entrust the decision to name the government that will conduct the affairs of the country for the following four or five years. There is no doubt in our minds that when we go back to the people they can make a decision for themselves on how they shall be governed and I think we are presuming a great deal when we decide that they cannot make a decision on how and where they will buy the products and merchandise they require for their daily living. If we ever come to the point where we decide that we can make that kind of decision for the public, I think we are striking at the very roots and principles of the institutions on which our country is founded.
However, I will only say this further. It can be proven on analysis that trading stamps are nothing more than a means of persuading people to go into a certain store or market to purchase. If the public is given access to all the facts of what is involved in this promotion, the opportunity to make its own decisions and to understand perhaps any merits there may be in the system as well as the demerits, I think that in due course an educated public will take care of this problem for itself.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE OF PUBLIC OPINION GALLUP POLL OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am greatly impressed by the number of people who are now using stamps of various kinds as a method of selling free enterprise. While it may be a form of free enterprise, we believe there are many problems arising from that practice that are not in keeping with free enterprise, if that phrase means competitive enterprise.
I visited a number of stores because I was concerned about the statement that was made the other day by the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) in which she said that the women of the country were very much in favour of having these trading stamps. I visited some of the grocery stores
[Mr. Fleming (Okanagan-Revelstoke) J
and several other small stores in order to find out whether or not they were in favour of these trading stamps and, if so, why.
In one small store I picked up a catalogue. Certainly it was a nice catalogue. I saw in it a great deal of valuable merchandise. I also picked up a little stamp book. The dealer from which I obtained it was interested in giving me the catalogue and the stamp book. Then I asked him his opinion. I said, "I should like to know whether you are in favour of the stamps, whether they have helped your business and whether you would like to carry on with them." He said to me, "Do you own a store?" I said, "No, I do not own a store". He said, "I am afraid I cannot tell you that. You will have to see the company that supplies me with the stamps". He did not want to discuss the matter at all. He may have had an opinion or he may not have had but he was not saying anything.
I looked at this little book. It is quite fancy in itself when it is empty. It has some interesting pictures in it. On the other side it has a number of quotations. Some of them-they are all along the same line-are quite interesting. Here is one:
Hurrah for Hannah Housewife She's really very wise She always shops at Gold Bond Stores And saves each time she buys.
Here is another one:
Here's a way to help your friends,
Says thrifty Sandy Saver.
Tell them to save Gold Bond Stamps And do them all a favour!
I would suggest that the people who are receiving this favour are probably the Gold Bond Company more than anyone else. It seems that this is a way they have of talking to the women. The women all show some interest in it.
We have been told that the C.C.F. want to legislate against the wishes of the people themselves and that sometimes we want to put into effect legislation because it is good for the people whether the people like it or not. I think that all we are suggesting is that if these things are free and if you are getting something for nothing, the C.C.F. would be more in favour of that happening than would anyone else I know of. I think it is also the contention of all hon. members who have spoken that somebody is going to pay for these premiums, these nicely coloured catalogues, and these fancy little books.
I am quite sure that Mr. Loeb is not in the business of retailing food and other merchandise throughout the Ottawa valley just in order to give you something for nothing. The reason that he went into the stamp company and is now president of it is that there is something in it for Mr. Loeb. I am quite

sure that somebody is going to pay for them because these stamps are not redeemable at the bank. The consumer is not going to get anything out of them for nothing. Somebody is going to pay for them and I am quite sure that everybody will agree that it is the consumer. We are of the opinion that the consumer does not always know that he-or she, in the main-is paying for the stamps which the public are told continually are giving them premiums for nothing.
I had an interesting conversation early this evening with a young lady who I understand is the public relations official for a number of these stamp companies which have got together and hired her to do a survey. In talking to her I was quite interested in learning that in six hours she was able to get 1000 signatures on a petition asking the provincial government to allow these stamps to be used in the stores and that she did this without a great deal of effort on her part. I do not think this proves that what we are trying to do is wrong. It just proves, as the hon. member for York-Humber pointed out the other day, that women may look at things in a different way.
In introducing this legislation I think the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) had in mind not only the legislative side of this question and some of the legalities and illegalities that are connected with it, some of which have been tried in the provincial courts and some that may be referred to the Supreme Court of Canada, but I think he was also taking into consideration the moral aspects of it. I think this is where the disagreement comes in, that we believe that if a thing is not good for somebody, even if it makes money for other people, that does not necessarily make it any better. If these companies are going to put out these stamps and say, "This will cost you money; somebody will have to pay for it, and it will be you", that is all right. If the wife wants to take the money her husband gives her and put away a certain amount of it as a saving and at the end of six months come home with a lamp, she can say to her husband, "This is something which I bought, and I bought it because I was sharp enough to deal at a store supplying stamps which allows me to get this kind of premium."
However, if we are being continually handed the propaganda from the various stores that they are giving away something for nothing, then I think this would be as dishonest as if we were to sell cotton shirts and say that they were 100 per cent pure wool. There are laws in Canada to prohibit that particular scheme, and I think there should be restrictions to prevent schemes taking place in this other field.
Criminal Code
I notice that the particular book I have, and others, have come before the royal commission on price spreads, and they point out on page 52 of the Stewart report that the retailers' obligation is to purchase the stamps from the stamp company, usually in batches of 20,000 at $20 a batch. A batch usually represents $1,000 of retail sales. Apparently the cost of trading stamp plans to the retailers is equivalent to about 2 per cent of the sales.
It has been pointed out this afternoon by a number of speakers that it represents only a cost of 2 per cent. But they may not have read the next sentence, which goes on to say that executive and trade opinion is that the retailer requires an increase of at least 20 per cent in his dollar sales volume if the plan is to be judged a success. In other words, unless he can increase his over-all volume of sales by 20 per cent somebody is going to have to pay for this program directly, and it will probably be paid for by the consumer because of resultant higher cost of produce.
It is also a fact, which is not contested by anyone, that if all the stores in a particular area subscribe to one or another of these plans, then obviously the advantage to the consumer which may accrue where the volume increases beyond 20 per cent will not be lost, and each one of the retail agents will be stuck with a plan which he will have to continue over a period of time, and he will have no way of unloading this type of advertisement or gimmick.
It has also been said that most of this 2 per cent will go back to the consumer himself in the form of these plans. I would suggest that this is not my experience with the plan, because having been in two or three of the large grocery stores of today, and having done so myself on other occasions as a transient, in most cases these people not collecting that particular kind of stamp say, "I don't want the stamps", and they give them to somebody else in the line-up, or give them to the girl behind the cash register.
I suggest that beyond this there are many people who take these stamps home and never do anything with them. This is a complete loss, and there is no value at all in the argument that they are getting something which they have already paid for; if they get the trading stamps and do not take them back, they are not even getting what they consider they have paid for.
There was an interesting presentation of this subject by William Dennison, member of the board of control, Toronto, where he pointed out the case of a man he talked to who had met a particular problem in his dealings with these stamps. One pensioner wrote

Criminal Code
that he had carefully pasted some 2,290 trading stamps in a book supplied for that purpose. He spent about $229 in that store to get these stamps. He bought four bottles of glue costing $1.20, and he and his wife wasted many hours neatly pasting these stamps in the book. All he was offered in return for his labour was three ordinary cups and saucers worth from fifty cents to $1. This is one of the problems with these trading stamps. If you do not collect a fantastically large number of them, you do not get anything of value, and while probably you can get something for one hundred stamp books, it would not be worth the bother of getting them.
In glancing over this particular catalogue I will agree with those who have said that in the main it is merchandise of well known companies and worth-while merchandise of name brands. But I would suggest that those who are connected with one of these wholesalers could get this merchandise a great deal cheaper if they wished and in turn could give it to their customers at a largely reduced price compared with the price quoted in this book. Just to take one example, you can get a thirty ounce thermos bottle for one and one fifth books, which would amount to $4 worth of premiums. So this could be bought at a cheaper price than you are having to pay for it, and I would say there are no advantages in buying it this way. It is not a wholesale proposition; the catalogue is calculated on the full retail price.
I suggest that if we are faced with the problem of women not knowing what they should do, if we as men consider them to be inefficient in their buying habits, then I think we have to support this legislation to protect our women folk against themselves.

I am certainly not suggesting that, no. I am suggesting that probably a man supplying money for the groceries would consider his money better spent than if his wife were buying a number of the premiums contained in this book.
Then we go from that point to another, which is probably the crux of the whole matter, and that is whether or not this advertising the women are paying attention to is false advertising or not. I think this matter was given consideration in the report of the royal commission on price spreads by Dr. Stewart. On page 36 he had this to say: The ultimate misconception to which people can be led is that anything in the market is "free".
If consumers are misled by being induced to buy something which is said to be "better" when it is not, they may never find out. Further, we are 
reluctant to accept the argument that, if consumers find they have been misled, the lesson to be learned is to use better judgment next time. As we have pointed out, in the case of a new product, the consumer cannot tell whether or not she wants it until after the purchase has been made. For this reason, we feel that any argument that condones misleading advertising indicates a cynical disregard for the welfare of the consumer.
It is my contention that this is exactly what is happening in the advertising which is taking place in connection with these stamp programs. On every page of this bulletin you will find a reference to getting something for nothing, and I am suggesting that there is nothing for nothing. If people are to be told: you will be able to have this merchandise, but what you buy will cost 2 per cent more, then well and good. But if we allow people to think that they are getting something for nothing, then in my opinion this is advertising as false as any which already comes under the act. Accordingly I suggest that we prohibit the use of the trading stamps as the province of Alberta has done, and I suggest this could best be accomplished through the method advocated by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard).

put in our Criminal Code, the basic law oi our country, such a trivial thing as a provision concerning trading stamps.
Actually, as the hon. member tor Saskatoon (Mr. Jones) said this afternoon, trading stamps are already illegal in this country. The reason is that back at the turn of the century stamp salesmen came to this country from the United States and sold the unsuspecting merchants this idea of trading stamps. Then when the time came around to collect the premiums the stamp salesmen had decamped. So the legislators of that day-1905-decided that the public was being victimized and that something should be done about it. But nobody in this country today has said that the public is being victimized in this way at the present time in regard to trading stamps, and, if they are, I think there are other ways of dealing with the question rather than by incorporating this inconsequential provision into our Criminal Code. One of those ways would be to oblige the trading stamp companies to bond themselves. That would protect the public.
There are some who say that these stamps are just a fad, and this may be true. I would not be surprised if it were true. What will happen? Some ingenious advertising man or promotion man will dream up another gimmick and everybody will rise up in wrath and say: these poor women are being fooled or duped. Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest this afternoon and this evening to the many speeches on the bill concerning trading stamps. At this time I should like to say a few words. In my remarks I shall take a little different approach to the problem than has been taken in the house today. I personally feel that it is of major importance to deal with this bill and that it should have earnest consideration of hon. members.
It has been suggested here today that the government should not have any part of or take any part in a case of this kind; but it is of major importance when one is dealing with the welfare and future of 300,000 small businesses. This figure is taken from the 1951 census and excludes small contractors. Perhaps it is a very conservative estimate. It also has to do with over one million of our workers.
As members of parliament, Mr. Speaker, we must remember that it is also important to the government, when one considers that every one of the small businessmen pays municipal taxes, provincial taxes, federal taxes and income tax. We should also remember the large number of people employed by various wholesale houses, warehouses, and the travellers whom they employ who are continually on the roads, staying at our hotels, motels and summer resorts and who are each and every day buying their meals in the different places along the road and purchasing motor products. Then there are the number of cars, trucks and railroads whose facilities are used for the delivery of this merchandise in Canada. Not to be excluded is the gasoline tax derived from all those vehicles.
A major fact also is that almost every dollar of the money spent by the small merchant is recirculated in Canada. That means the profits are not going to another country.
I should like to point out that at least the majority of our small businessmen want to buy and do buy Canadian-manufactured goods. It is my opinion that if these gimmicks are allowed to continue it will matter not whether the goods are manufactured in Canada. Price only will be the guide. I should like to point out that this is one way in which business and money can be spread throughout the entire country, thus giving small business a chance of survival. Therefore I feel personally that trading stamps should be abolished.

maintopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE OF PUBLIC OPINION GALLUP POLL OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of interest to the pros and cons with respect to the matter of trading stamps. Having in mind all the speeches I have heard today, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) for taking such an objective attitude. I believe we should take an objective stand. Personally I think the subject matter is ultra vires of the federal parliament. In my opinion it falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces under property and civil rights.
At the present time several cases in Manitoba have not been heard by the court of appeal and we do not know what the decisions will be. Hon. members who support the bill have referred to the fact that the province of Alberta has prohibited trading stamps, and we must be sure whether it is the federal parliament or the provincial legislatures that have jurisdiction.
Nevertheless, we have the bill before us and I think we should take an objective attitude toward it. We should analyse it from all sides. I should like to take the other side of the question and defend the poor stamp. I do not do so just to be different but because I feel that both sides of the question should be heard. We know who are opposed to trading stamps. We know that especially in the big centres the chain stores, in order to attract business, have entered into the scheme of giving so many trading stamps for every dollar of goods purchased. This hurts somebody but every promotional scheme, every promotional device, hurts somebody.
To refer again to the speech of the hon. member for York-Humber, I believe that we are creating a tempest in a teapot. If this scheme or gimmick is abolished some other smart scheme will be introduced. If it is to the detriment of consumers it will die a natural death and we should not clutter up the ' Criminal Code any more than it is already. This is a promotional scheme or device and we live in a free country with a free economy. Every business has to fight for every dollar it gets and various schemes are used. Trading stamps are just one scheme. Are we going to abolish all of them? I am going to list a few of them. What about newspaper advertising? We see whole page advertisements in the daily press, and they must cost a pretty penny. Who pays for them? You and I, the consumers, only we do not see it. We get one of these trading stamps for every ten cents worth of goods purchased and some people want to treat this as a crime. I do not want to mention the store I get them from because that would be an advertisement for the store.

Criminal Code
But who pays for the pages and pages of advertising of groceries, dry-goods and everything else? Whom does it hurt? I will tell you. It hurts the little merchant, the little grocer who cannot afford to advertise. Then we have advertising on radio and television, which was also referred to by the hon. member for York-Humber. I think she took part of my speech away.

maintopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE OF PUBLIC OPINION GALLUP POLL OF CANADA
speechtext: That is a woman for you.

maintopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE OF PUBLIC OPINION GALLUP POLL OF CANADA
speechtext:
Whom do you think pays for the time of that sweet lady on television who holds in her hand a pack of cigarettes and sings, "Ask for-" or "Smoke..."? Who pays for that if not you and I? Every customer who buys that particular product pays for it. Why is there this advertising on radio and television? It is a promotional gimmick or device to get customers interested in the particular product, to get them to buy. Trading stamps are just another promotional device and I see absolutely no difference between them and newspaper or radio and television advertising.
If we are so concerned about the cost of the product being increased on this account, we might as well make it illegal for people to advertise in the newspapers and on radio and on television. There are other promotional devices that competition has compelled business to use. Let me give an example. I do not know whether those who live in the large centres get them but I know that in rural Manitoba envelopes containing coupons are received by the householders from time to time. With a coupon I can go to the store and get a certain brand of cereal for ten cents less. The coupon is worth ten cents if I buy that cereal, or it may be a coupon for a certain brand of toilet soap, soap flakes or something else. The coupon is worth so much. I have seen little storekeepers up to their necks trying to sort out these coupons at the end of the month because they get a refund on them.
But who pays for them if not the customer? It costs money to print the coupons. There is also the cost of postage stamps and envelopes to send them to the householder. We pay for these things. We might as well make these schemes illegal. There are also coupons for the purchase of tea, coffee and so on. We have seen advertisements that if you buy a tankful of gas you will get a carton of soft drinks or something else free. What is the reason for that? Is that not a promotional device? You can call it a gimmick or whatever you like, but business must fight for every dollar it can possibly get from consumers. In the case of all these devices I ask the question again, who pays? You pay and I pay.

Criminal Code
At the beginning of my address I said that we know those who are against trading stamps. But I wonder how many members have noticed in today's Ottawa Journal a story with the headline, "1,000 City Women Join Fight to Keep Trading Stamps". I believe that for every woman who objects there must be ten who are in favour, and the attitude of these women is becoming known. They are organizing throughout the country.
I believe in our free economy, and I believe in the integrity and common sense of our women who do most of the buying. They have a choice of the stores they want to patronize. They can very quickly detect whether or not they are being fleeced. They can very quickly detect whether or not, by virtue of receiving trading stamps, the quality of the goods is lower or the price is higher.
I have not heard any statistics, and we could have had statistics from those who wanted to support this bill, as to what happens to prices in the non-stamp stores. Mark you, Mr. Speaker, I would consider it a crime to permit the issue or receipt of trading stamps if it could be proven to my satisfaction, and the satisfaction of all Canadians that the customer is being fooled into believing he is getting something for nothing. Some reference was made to that by some hon. members. I could quote statistics given by Dr. James Phillips before the United States committee on agriculture, and who said that the customer does receive value for these trading stamps and the value he receives is anywhere from 1.55 per cent to 2.29 per cent on every dollar spent in the store. Unless it can be proven that the customer gets nothing, that he is fooled, then you cannot make this a crime. Any provision you place in the Criminal Code immediately creates a crime punishable by either a fine or a jail term.
Another point which I should like cleared up before I would condemn the present practice is whether the customer is cheated through the use of stamps. Are we so gullible and ignorant that we do not catch on? Are our wives and daughters so ignorant and foolish that they do not catch on to any scheme that tries to cheat them out of a hard earned dollar? I do not believe there was a single address during the course of the day which gave any indication that that was the case, or at least did not give us statistics to prove that was the case.
We have heard charges that this practice increases the cost of doing business. To whom does it increase the cost? Does it not increase the cost of doing business if a firm decides to take a full page advertisement in a daily

newspaper? Does it not increase the cost of doing business if a merchant remodels his store and puts in self-service shelves? Does it not increase the cost of his business if he puts in plate glass windows or if he hires extra boys to carry out the ladies' parcels to their cars? Is that not just another promotional device? These things do increase costs, but to whom? It has to be proven that this increase is all passed on to the consumer, and this has not been proven. I do not believe we have received any statistics on that point at all.
Those who promote these trading stamps naturally depend on an increased volume of business, and thus increased profits and increased employment. Certainly this hurts somebody. Every promotional scheme in a competitive economy such as ours always hurts somebody. When I started legal practice in my town, every time a new lawyer came in it was hurting me. This was competition, and it was taking business away from me. Every new merchant who comes in is competition and hurts somebody. Are we going to make it illegal to expand or are we going to kill competition when competition is the very essence of our economic life?
Another point upon which I would have liked to have some proof is, does the retailer increase prices? I would have liked to hear from those who would like to make this a crime-provided of course the matter is intra vires of the dominion parliament-whether or not the retailer increases his price by virtue of the fact he handles stamps. Does a pound of coffee of the same brand and quality cost the same in a store that hands out trading stamps as it does in a store that does not give trading stamps? If it costs the same, then who is being hurt? These trading stamps do have value, and if they have value then the customer is not hurt, and there are more customers than storekeepers.
I could name other devices, Mr. Speaker, which are practised by our retailers and even by the wholesale trade. I know of chewing gum manufacturers who come along with a deal and if a merchant buys so much of that particular product they give him a bathroom scale. I have actually seen that scheme in operation. This is another promotional scheme. Are we going to make that illegal as well because it hurts somebody? If your store is loaded up with that particular brand of chewing gum, then other chewing gum manufacturers have not much chance of selling their product to your store. That is a device we have. Then there is the device of giving an exclusive agency to one storekeeper, one out of ten, who will sell a particular manufactured product, whether it is a washing

machine, radio or something else. Are we going to make that illegal too? It hurts somebody. It is not fair for one Tom Jones, or whoever he is, to have exclusive selling privileges for that product. Are we going to make it illegal?
There are many other instances I could mention. Some people get so fired up by their missionary zeal to sponsor something that they would like to see the government take action upon that they want this practice declared a crime right away. Put everybody in jail. You have to consider these things in an objective manner, as the hon. member for York-Humber has done, and look at them from all sides. Let us find out first whether the matter is entirely within the jurisdiction of the provinces. If it is entirely within the jurisdiction of the provinces, then we certainly have wasted a wonderful afternoon and evening in this house. Supposing it is not within the jurisdiction of the provinces, Mr. Speaker, I think it is too trivial a matter with which to clutter up our Criminal Code. I believe that Canadian buyers, and our women, are intelligent enough to see on which side their bread is buttered. They will go where they can buy the best quality goods at the best prices, regardless of whether or not they are getting trading stamps.
